abstract: Arm separation is an important technical tool in the study of critical and near-critical planar percolation systems. When combined with RSW estimates, it proves quasi-multiplicativity of arm-event probabilities, links the derivatives of different events and allows the identification of universal arm exponents. We provide a very generic statement of arm separation that applies to arbitrary planar percolation models. Our argument is based on exploring configurations conditioned on the existence of arms in such a way that "exposed" arms are revealed with positive probability. The exploration algorithm is independent of the percolation model and applies to all polychromatic arm events. As an application, we prove a strong arm-separation result for critical planar FK-percolation.
label: arXiv:2611.26458v1

summary.background: ['Percolation: sites or edges are randomly open or closed, and the question is when open clusters span large distances.', 'Critical point: the threshold probability at which large connected clusters first appear; behaviour there is scale-invariant.', 'Arm events: events that several disjoint paths of given colours (open or closed) cross a region from one place to another.', 'RSW (Russo–Seymour–Welsh) estimates: bounds saying crossing events are not too unlikely across scales.', 'Quasi-multiplicativity and arm exponents: probabilities of multiple arms factor up to constants across scales, and the decay rates are universal numbers.', 'FK-percolation: a generalisation of percolation tied to the Potts model in statistical physics.', 'Conditioning and exploration: revealing random configuration step by step to control dependence between events.']
summary.one_liner: The paper proves a model-independent arm-separation statement for arbitrary planar percolation models, using an exploration argument that reveals arms with positive probability, and applies it to get a strong arm-separation result for critical planar FK-percolation.
summary.plain: Percolation is a simple random model of a porous material: each spot is open or closed at random, and one asks when open paths connect distant places. The authors study how several separate open or closed paths ('arms') can be made to stay apart from one another in a plane, a property that underpins precise estimates of how likely such connections are near the critical point. They give a general version of this separation property that does not depend on the particular random model, and they check it on a more complicated model called FK-percolation, which comes from statistical physics. The abstract does not report numerical values or further consequences beyond the statement and this application.
summary.why: Arm-separation results are a standard tool for deriving exponents and scaling behaviour in two-dimensional critical random systems, so a statement that works across many models could make those tools easier to reuse. The abstract does not say how widely the result will be adopted, so its impact beyond this setting is uncertain.

title: Generic arm separation for planar percolation models

abstract: We prove dynamical edge universality for three families of interacting particle systems for every $β>0$: $β$-Dyson Brownian motion with an analytic potential, weighted $β$-corners processes, and a class of discrete-time Markov chains. Our results apply to general non-equilibrium initial data and show that the Airy$_β$ line ensemble emerges at positive times whenever the limiting density has a regular square-root edge. More precisely, after centering at the moving deterministic edge and rescaling space and time on the $n^{-2/3}$ and $n^{-1/3}$ scales, respectively, the trajectories of the top $k$ particles converge jointly in distribution to the top $k$ curves of the Airy$_β$ line ensemble, for every fixed $k$, in the topology of uniform convergence on compact time intervals. The proof combines dynamical loop equations with characteristic-flow estimates to establish local laws near the moving edge and upper bounds on the extremal particle. We then identify the stochastic evolution of every subsequential limit of the rescaled Stieltjes transform and establish convergence through the pole-evolution characterization of the Airy$_β$ line ensemble.
label: arXiv:2611.25364v1

summary.background: ['Random matrices and eigenvalues: a large matrix with random entries has eigenvalues that spread into a limiting density, and this paper is about the particles at the edge of that spread.', 'The parameter β: it controls how strongly the particles repel each other (β=1, 2, 4 correspond to classical symmetric, Hermitian and quaternion ensembles).', 'Universality: many different random models share the same small-scale limiting behaviour, so the detailed model matters less than general features.', 'Airy process / line ensemble: the scaling limit of edge particles, a random infinite collection of continuous curves; the Airy_β version generalizes the Airy process to every β.', 'Dyson Brownian motion: a stochastic process in which eigenvalues evolve in time as diffusing particles with mutual repulsion.', 'Stieltjes transform and loop equations: analytic tools that encode the empirical particle density through a complex function and yield algebraic identities satisfied by moments of the system.', 'Scaling: space is rescaled by n^{-2/3} and time by n^{-1/3}, the standard edge scales.']
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that for every β>0, three families of interacting particle systems (β-Dyson Brownian motion with analytic potential, weighted β-corners processes, and a class of discrete-time Markov chains), started from general non-equilibrium data, have their top k particles near the moving spectral edge converge, after edge-centering and n^{-2/3} space / n^{-1/3} time rescaling, to the top k curves of the Airy_β line ensemble, using dynamical loop equations and characteristic-flow estimates.
summary.plain: The paper studies systems of many randomly moving particles that repel each other, such as eigenvalues of large random matrices evolving over time. When the particles spread out in a square-root-shaped pattern, the particles at the outer edge behave in a universal way, and the authors prove this holds over time for three model families, starting from fairly general initial configurations. Zooming in on the leading few particles at the edge, their paths converge to a known random object called the Airy_β line ensemble.
summary.why: It extends edge universality, a central theme in random matrix theory, from equilibrium snapshots to the full time evolution of the particles, covering all values of the repulsion parameter β>0. Its relevance to other areas rests on the universality claim, but the abstract does not discuss specific applications.

title: Dynamical edge universality and the Airy$_β$ line ensemble

abstract: We prove that the Lawson minimal surface $ξ_{g,1}$ in $S^3$ is strongly stable for the Willmore bending energy $W$ and remains strongly $W$-stable in $S^n$ for every $n \geq4$; our proof starts with a new lower bound on the area-index of $ξ_{m,k}$ for $m\geq k>1$. Next we observe that each of the $ξ_{m,k}$ and the Karcher-Pinkall-Sterling minimal surfaces in $S^3$, as well as the equilateral minimal torus in $S^5$, is the unique $W$-minimizer in its conformal class, up to Möbius transformations of $S^n$. Finally, we show that although the equilateral minimal torus is $W$-stable in $S^n$ for every $n \geq5$, it is neither strongly $W$-stable nor a local $W$-minimizer: it has a 2-dimensional space of $W$-Jacobi fields on which almost everywhere the third-variation of $W$ is nonzero.
label: arXiv:2611.26238v1

summary.one_liner: We prove that the Lawson minimal surface $ξ_{g,1}$ in $S^3$ is strongly stable for the Willmore bending energy $W$ and remains strongly $W$-stable in $S^n$ for every $n \geq4$; our proof starts with a new lower bound on the area-index of $ξ_{m,k}$ for $m\geq k>1$.

title: Willmore stability of minimal surfaces in the n-sphere

abstract: We show that the generalized Polterovich submanifold $L_{0, 2}^P$ in $\mathbb{C}P^3(\sqrt{2})$ and the Chekanov-Oakley-Usher Lagrangian $L_{1, 2}^{Q, \mathrm{Ch}}$ in the quadric $Q^4(\sqrt{2})$ are displaceable. Since $L_{0, 2}^P$ and $L_{1, 2}^{Q, \mathrm{Ch}}$ are in the zero level set of the moment maps of the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-actions on $\mathbb{C}P^3(\sqrt{2})$ and $Q^4(\sqrt{2})$, the main idea is to construct Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms mapping $L_{0, 2}^P$ and $L_{1, 2}^{Q, \mathrm{Ch}}$ to nonzero level sets of the moment maps.
label: arXiv:2611.25699v1

summary.one_liner: We show that the generalized Polterovich submanifold $L_{0, 2}^P$ in $\mathbb{C}P^3(\sqrt{2})$ and the Chekanov-Oakley-Usher Lagrangian $L_{1, 2}^{Q, \mathrm{Ch}}$ in the quadric $Q^4(\sqrt{2})$ are displaceable.

title: Displaceability of monotone Lagrangians in $\mathbb{C}P^3(\sqrt{2})$ and $Q^4(\sqrt{2})$

abstract: In this paper we prove a theorem on the unique solvability of the Cauchy problem for a stochastic partial differential equation driven by the fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index $H>\frac{1}{4}$.
label: arXiv:2611.26580v1

summary.one_liner: In this paper we prove a theorem on the unique solvability of the Cauchy problem for a stochastic partial differential equation driven by the fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index $H>\frac{1}{4}$.

title: Existence and Uniqueness of Mild Solutions to Rough Stochastic Partial Differential Equations driven by Fractional Brownian Motion with Hurst Index $H > 1/4$

abstract: In this note, we improve the regularity of Hölder continuous stationary solutions with respect to inner variations which are harmonic outside their zero set. We obtain a $\sqrt{\log}$-Lipschitz estimate for a class of solutions allowing a generalized phase variable and including the two-phase problem. In the case of the one-phase problem, we can improve to Lipschitz regularity. In particular, we show that the initial Lipschitz assumption in the class of variational solutions considered by Kriventsov and Weiss can be replaced by any positive Hölder exponent
label: arXiv:2611.25345v1

summary.background: ['Partial differential equations: equations relating a function to its rates of change in several variables.', 'Free boundary problem: a problem in which the region where the solution is nonzero (or where phases differ) is itself unknown and must be determined.', 'Hölder continuity: a measure of smoothness, where an exponent between 0 and 1 controls how closely nearby values must match; Lipschitz is the case of bounded slope.', "Harmonic function: a solution of Laplace's equation, the classic smooth 'equilibrium' function.", 'Stationary solution with inner variations: a solution that does not change to first order under small reparametrizations of the domain, i.e. a critical point of an energy.', 'One-phase versus two-phase problems: whether the solution is zero on one side of the interface or takes two distinct nonzero regimes.', 'Regularity: how smooth a solution is guaranteed to be; here, how its gradient or continuity is controlled.']
summary.one_liner: The paper sharpens the regularity theory for Hölder-continuous stationary solutions of free boundary problems that are harmonic off their zero set, obtaining a √log-Lipschitz bound for a generalized phase-variable class (including the two-phase problem), a full Lipschitz bound in the one-phase case, and showing that a Lipschitz assumption in Kriventsov–Weiss's variational class can be weakened to any positive Hölder exponent.
summary.plain: Free boundary problems describe shapes where two regions (for example, a region with a substance and one without, or two different materials) meet along an interface whose position is part of the answer. This note asks how smooth the solutions must be when they are stationary, meaning they are balanced against small deformations of the domain. The authors show that a weaker starting assumption on smoothness suffices than was previously required, and they get a slightly weaker or stronger smoothness conclusion depending on whether there is one phase or two.
summary.why: Getting by with a weaker smoothness assumption makes the regularity result apply to a broader class of solutions, which matters for free boundary theory in general. I can only judge the significance from the abstract, so the wider impact is uncertain; the connections it may have to variational and geometric questions are not spelled out there.

title: On the regularity of stationary solutions to free boundary problems

abstract: We consider Hörmander oscillatory integral operators on $\mathbb{R}^n$. In particular, we are interested in proving bounds with dependence on the signature of the phase. The sharp universal range of $L^p\to L^p$ estimates was obtained for any given signature by the second author and Iliopoulou. Under the mild non-compression hypotheses on the phase introduced in Chen et al., we prove $L^p\to L^p$ estimates that go beyond this universal range in odd dimensions. We also obtain the sharp universal range of $L^p\to L^q$ estimates for odd $n$. The techniques are based on the breakthrough work of Wang--Wu on the Fourier restriction conjecture.
label: arXiv:2611.26265v1

summary.one_liner: We consider Hörmander oscillatory integral operators on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

title: Oscillatory integral operators of arbitrary signature: beyond the universal estimates

abstract: Let $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ be non-trivial closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space $\mathscr{H}$ such that $\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}=\{0\}$ and $\mathscr{M}+\mathscr{N}$ is dense in $\mathscr{H}$. We characterize when there exists an invertible operator on $\mathscr{H}$ which maps $\mathscr{M}$ onto $\mathscr{N}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ onto $\mathscr{M}$. We prove that such an operator exists if and only if $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ have a common algebraic complement. This happens if and only if either neither of the operators $(I-P)Q$ and $(I-Q)P$ is compact, or $P-Q$ is compact and $\dim(\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}^\perp)=\dim(\mathscr{M}^\perp\cap\mathscr{N})$, where $P$ and $Q$ are the orthogonal projections onto $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$. Moreover, the operator can be chosen to be an involution. Consequently, the group of collineations of the diamond lattice $\{\{0\},\mathscr{M},\mathscr{N},\mathscr{H}\}$ which fix $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ is always complemented in the group of all its collineations.
label: arXiv:2611.25622v1

summary.one_liner: Let $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ be non-trivial closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space $\mathscr{H}$ such that $\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}=\{0\}$ and $\mathscr{M}+\mathscr{N}$ is dense in $\mathscr{H}$.

title: Collineations of the diamond lattice in a Hilbert space

abstract: In 1926, Nevanlinna (Acta Math. {\bf 48} (1926), no. 3-4, 367-391) proved that if two distinct and non-constant meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$ share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3,$ $a_4$ CM in the complex plane, where $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3,$ $a_4$ are four distinct complex values in the extended complex plane, then $f$ is a Möbius transformation of $g$, two of the shared values, say $a_1$ and $a_2$, are Picard exceptional values, and the cross ratio $\left(a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4\right)=-1.$ Later on, Gundersen (Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. {\bf 277} (1983), no. 2, 545-567. Correction: {\bf 304} (1987), 847-850) proved that if two non-constant meromorphic functions share two values CM and share two other values IM, then the functions share all four values CM. In 1992, Gundersen (Complex Var. Elliptic Equ. {\bf 20} (1992), no. 1-4, 99-106) proposed the following famous question: if two non-constant meromorphic functions share three distinct values IM and share a fourth value CM, then do the functions necessarily share all four values CM? This question is a long-standing question in the studies of the Nevanlinna's value distribution theory of meromorphic functions, and has not been completely resolved by now. In this paper, we completely resolve the question, and prove that if two distinct and non-constant meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$ share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ IM and $\infty$ CM, where $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ are three distinct and finite complex values in the complex plane, then $f$ and $g$ also share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ CM.
label: arXiv:2611.25948v1

summary.background: ['Meromorphic function: a function of a complex variable that is holomorphic except for isolated poles, which are its only infinities.', "Sharing a value: two functions share a value a if f(z)=a exactly when g(z)=a; 'IM' (ignoring multiplicity) only compares the points, while 'CM' (counting multiplicity) also matches how many times each point is hit.", 'Nevanlinna value distribution theory: the study of how often a meromorphic function takes given values, measured by counting functions and characteristic functions.', "Picard exceptional value: a value that a function omits entirely, or takes only finitely often in the sense of Picard's theorems.", "Cross ratio and Möbius transformation: the cross ratio is a four-point invariant of the Riemann sphere, and a Möbius transformation is a rational map of degree one that preserves it; these appear in Nevanlinna's classical four-value result.", "Gundersen's question: a 1992 open problem asking whether three values shared IM plus a fourth shared CM forces all four to be shared CM."]
summary.one_liner: The paper settles Gundersen's 1992 question by proving that two non-constant meromorphic functions sharing three finite values IM and infinity CM must also share those three finite values CM, which upgrades the sharing relation without extra hypotheses.
summary.plain: The question concerns two functions of a complex variable that take the same specific values at the same points, either counting multiplicity or ignoring it. Gundersen asked in 1992 whether agreeing on three values loosely and a fourth value strictly forces agreement on all four strictly, and this has been open for decades. The authors show that, for the special case where the fourth value is infinity, the answer is yes: agreement on three values loosely plus infinity strictly implies agreement on the three values strictly as well.
summary.why: It closes a well-known open problem in value distribution theory, so it matters to specialists in that area. The abstract covers only the special case with infinity as the strict value, so it does not by itself settle the general form of Gundersen's question for an arbitrary fourth value; that scope should be kept in view.

title: On the solution of a question for meromorphic functions sharing three values IM and a fourth value CM in the complex plane

abstract: We study the single matrix point interpolation problem for positive real matrix valued functions on the right half-plane, both in the single variable setting and in the noncommutative multivariable setting. In the single variable case, a careful analysis is done for when the solution may or must have a pole at infinity. In the multivariable setting, as the pole structure at infinity can be more complicated, we focus on the case when there is no pole at infinity. The results also yield numerical algorithms for finding a solution.
label: arXiv:2611.26240v1

summary.background: ['Interpolation: finding a function that matches given values at given points.', 'Matrix-valued functions: each output is a grid of numbers, and matrices need not commute when multiplied.', 'Positive real functions: functions whose real part is nonnegative on a region, common in circuit and control theory.', 'Right half-plane: the set of complex numbers with positive real part.', "Pole at infinity: a point where the function's size grows without bound as the input goes far out; whether this is permitted determines which solutions exist.", 'Noncommutative several variables: functions of several matrix-valued inputs where the order of multiplication matters.']
summary.one_liner: The paper studies matrix-valued interpolation for positive real (odd) functions on the right half-plane, in one variable and in noncommutative several variables, characterizing when solutions may or must have a pole at infinity and giving numerical algorithms.
summary.plain: The problem asks for a smooth rule-based function that takes prescribed matrix values at a chosen point and also stays 'positive' on a half of the complex plane, a constraint that often arises in engineering and systems theory. The authors work out, in the one-variable case, exactly when such a function is allowed or forced to blow up at infinity, and in the several-variable case (with matrices that do not commute) they handle the simpler situation where it does not blow up. Their results also come with numerical methods for actually computing a solution.
summary.why: Interpolation with positivity constraints underlies many problems in control, signal processing and system identification, so clear criteria for solvability and a computational route are useful. The noncommutative multivariable extension links the work to operator theory and realization theory, though the abstract does not show how far the results reach beyond this setting.

title: Matrix-point interpolation for positive real odd functions in one and several variables

abstract: We consider vector-valued magnetic Schrödinger operators $-Δ_{a} +V$ with magnetic potential ${a}\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$ and electric potential $V$ given by a symmetric and positive semidefinite $m\times m$ matrix-valued function whose entries belong to $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Assuming that $\|\operatorname{curl} {a}(\cdot)\|\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb{R}^m} + V$ belongs to a certain matrix reverse Hölder class, we characterize necessary and sufficient conditions under which the spectrum of $-Δ_{a} +V$ is discrete, and study the eigenvalue asymptotics and exponential decay of eigenfunctions.
label: arXiv:2611.26479v1

summary.one_liner: We consider vector-valued magnetic Schrödinger operators $-Δ_{a} +V$ with magnetic potential ${a}\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$ and electric potential $V$ given by a symmetric and positive semidefinite $m\times m$ matrix-valued function whose entries belong to $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)$.

title: Spectral asymptotics for vector-valued magnetic Schrödinger operators

abstract: We prove that every unital surjective complex-linear spectral isometry between complex unital semisimple Banach algebras is a Jordan isomorphism, thereby giving an affirmative answer to the spectrum-preserving form of Kaplansky's conjecture. We also characterize surjective complex-linear maps between arbitrary unital Banach algebras that preserve invertibility in either direction, satisfy either spectral inclusion, or preserve the spectral radius. In particular, for a complex-linear bijection between semisimple Banach algebras, preservation of invertibility in either direction implies preservation in both directions, and either spectral inclusion implies equality of spectra, even without assuming unitality. As an application, we study preservers of the Fredholm essential spectrum and essential spectral radius.
label: arXiv:2611.26462v1

summary.one_liner: We prove that every unital surjective complex-linear spectral isometry between complex unital semisimple Banach algebras is a Jordan isomorphism, thereby giving an affirmative answer to the spectrum-preserving form of Kaplansky's conjecture.

title: Spectral isometries and invertibility preservers on Banach algebras

abstract: For any given irreducible polynomial $f(x)=a_0+a_1\cdot x+\cdots+a_d\cdot x^d\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, we study the structure of finite groups $(G,\cdot)$ that have a fixed-point-free-automorphism $α$ satisfying the condition \[ \{g^{a_0}\cdotα(g)^{a_1}\cdotsα^d(g)^{a_d}\mid g\in G\}=\{1\}. \] We show that such a group $G$ is nilpotent of class at most $d^{2^d}$, provided that $|G|$ is coprime to an explicit, non-zero, integer invariant $ι(f(x))$ of $f(x)$. We do this by extending the solutions of the Frobenius conjecture. We also extend the solution of the restricted Burnside problem in prime exponent and the classification of the $n$-abelian groups.
label: arXiv:2611.25886v1

title: Finite groups with a fixed-point-free automorphism satisfying an irreducible identity

abstract: We classify the nonsolvable finite groups that are critical with respect to the spectrum of the symmetric group $S_{10}$. Up to isomorphism, there are exactly two such groups: $S_{10}$ and $(A_9\times C_3)\rtimes C_2$, where the involution acts on $A_9$ by conjugation by a transposition and on $C_3$ by inversion. The quotient of any nonsolvable group with this spectrum by its solvable radical is almost simple. All possible simple socles are treated without assuming that the radical is nilpotent. The final cases, $L_3(4)$ and $A_6$, are excluded using the canonical subgroup $K=[R(G)\cap G^\infty,G^\infty]$, actions on chief factors, and the required element orders $9,20,30$. In the $A_6$ case, the final contradiction is the existence of an element of order $16$. Reproducible certificates accompany the character-table and matrix calculations.
label: arXiv:2611.25766v1

summary.one_liner: We classify the nonsolvable finite groups that are critical with respect to the spectrum of the symmetric group $S_{10}$.

title: Nonsolvable critical groups with the spectrum of $S_{10}$

abstract: Let $H$ be a quasi-triangular Hopf algebra of sqaure-free dimension over $\mathbb{C}$. In this note, we show that $H$ is semisimple and cocommutative. Equivalently, a braided finite tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ of square-free Frobenius--Perron dimension with a fiber functor is tensor equivalent to the representation category of a finite group.
label: arXiv:2611.25676v1

summary.one_liner: Let $H$ be a quasi-triangular Hopf algebra of sqaure-free dimension over $\mathbb{C}$.

title: On quasi-triangular Hopf algebras of square-free dimensions

abstract: We construct super analogues of the quantum groups of divided powers introduced by Lusztig. We call them super analogues because the Lie-theoretical data governing their structure is comparable to that of contragredient Lie superalgebras. Indeed, we show that they admit PBW-type bases parametrized by root systems of super type, and that they also have Lusztig isomorphisms giving a representation of the corresponding Weyl groupoids. Moreover, we prove that our super objects are equipped with a Frobenius-type morphism whose kernel is the Drinfeld double of a finite-dimensional Nichols algebra of super type, a super analogue of Lusztig's small quantum group, and whose cokernel is the enveloping algebra of the semisimple Lie algebra determined by the Cartan roots of the Nichols algebra. We carry out our construction within the framework of Nichols algebras of diagonal type, specifically, those whose braiding is obtained by specializing at a root of unity. This allows us to consider a divided power integral form inside a large quantum group of De Concini--Kac--Procesi type and then, via specialization, obtain our desired object.
label: arXiv:2611.26505v1

summary.one_liner: We construct super analogues of the quantum groups of divided powers introduced by Lusztig.

title: Super quantum groups of divided powers à la Lusztig

abstract: We determine the algebraic relations among full de Rham comparison periods of elliptic curves over finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_p$. The connected local monodromy group gives the transcendence degree and an explicit affine linear relation ideal for the full matrix in Fontaine's field $B_{\mathrm{dR}}$. After normalizing the holomorphic row and reducing to $\mathbb C_p$, the transcendence degree drops by one and the normalized determinant supplies the additional relation. Every polynomial relation of degree at most $d$ is detected modulo $t^{d+1}$. For $d\ge1$ this bound is sharp for each elliptic curve. A rational quasi-period row gives a Galois-stable Tate line. Together with an algebraic holomorphic period ratio it forces potential splitting, which identifies the exact ordinary CM obstruction. We compute the full Tate matrix. For ordinary non-CM curves with $p\ge5$, the standard quasi-period row is rational precisely at a zero of Katz's $E_{2,p}$. Away from the zeros the two full ratios are algebraically independent. At the zeros, a nonzero quasi-period and the normalized holomorphic ratio have algebraically independent images in $\mathbb C_p$. The complex question that motivates these results, the analogue for Drinfeld modules, and a conditional arithmetic consequence for Katz values complete the comparison.
label: arXiv:2611.25399v1

summary.one_liner: We determine the algebraic relations among full de Rham comparison periods of elliptic curves over finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_p$.

title: Rational Elliptic Period Relations Across Realizations: Complex Lattices, Local p-adic Periods, and Drinfeld Modules

abstract: The modular properties of holomorphic Eisenstein series for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and its congruence subgroups do not carry over to their primitives. Instead, the transformation of iterated Eisenstein integrals under congruence subgroups of level $N$ introduces inhomogeneous terms comprising (among others) cyclotomic multiple zeta values of level $N$. We combine iterated Eisenstein integrals for the congruence subgroups of level $N=2$ of arbitrary iteration depth with their complex conjugates and (single-valued) level-2 cyclotomic multiple zeta values such that they define non-holomorphic modular forms. Our construction of these so-called equivariant iterated Eisenstein integrals for $Γ(2)$ and $Γ_0(2)$ proceeds at the level of generating series that take values in an infinite-dimensional (pro-unipotent) Lie group and closely follow Brown's analogous construction in the $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ case. The required insertions of cyclotomic multiple zeta values are controlled by zeta generators for level 2 that normalise the corresponding (pro-nilpotent) Lie algebra of the generating series and whose Lie-bracket relations we determine systematically. Upon restriction to Eisenstein series of modular weight~2, we recover single-valued multiple polylogarithms on the genus 0 modular curve $Γ(2)\backslash \mathbb{H}$.
label: arXiv:2611.26597v1

summary.background: ['Modular forms: complex functions on the upper half-plane with transformation rules under a group of matrices (here SL_2(Z) and its subgroups).', 'Congruence subgroups of level N: subgroups defined by reducing matrix entries mod N; Γ(2) and Γ_0(2) are the level-2 cases.', 'Eisenstein series: standard explicit modular forms; their iterated integrals are repeated antiderivatives.', 'Multiple zeta values and cyclotomic variants: iterated sums or integrals producing special constants, with roots-of-unity versions at level N.', 'Non-holomorphic modular forms: modular objects that involve complex conjugation and are not holomorphic, needed to make the corrected objects transform cleanly.', 'Generating series and pro-unipotent Lie groups/algebras: a packaging device that encodes all iteration depths at once and tracks how the corrections compose.']
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs non-holomorphic modular objects, called equivariant iterated Eisenstein integrals, for the level-2 congruence subgroups Γ(2) and Γ_0(2), built from iterated Eisenstein integrals, their complex conjugates, and level-2 cyclotomic multiple zeta values, following Brown's SL_2(Z) construction.
summary.plain: Modular forms are highly symmetric functions on the complex upper half-plane, and their 'antiderivatives' (integrals) do not keep that symmetry on their own. This paper repairs the problem for a specific family of symmetry groups of level 2, by adding correction terms built from special constants called multiple zeta values, together with complex conjugates. The authors work with generating series valued in an infinite-dimensional algebraic group. When they restrict to the weight-2 case, they recover known single-valued multiple polylogarithms on a particular curve. The abstract does not state any further consequences beyond this construction.
summary.why: It extends a known construction from the full modular group to two important congruence subgroups, and it links iterated integrals of Eisenstein series to multiple polylogarithms and to physics-adjacent single-valued functions. The abstract does not explain the wider significance beyond these connections, and I have not checked how much new this is relative to prior work.

title: Equivariant iterated Eisenstein integrals for congruence subgroups of level 2

abstract: We study the specialization of Donaldson-Thomas virtual cycles for surface sheaves on a Calabi Yau threefold degenerating to a simple normal crossing threefold, composed of two quasi Fano threefolds glued along a common (double) divisor. The compactification of the two relative sheaf moduli spaces involves construction of suitable moduli space of sheaves on expanded degenerations of each quasi Fano variety. On a fixed expanded fiber the matching datum is an equivalence of the derived restrictions of the component sheaves. We identify the corresponding deformation complexes and give valuative and obstruction-theoretic hypotheses under which the specialized virtual class is a sum over marked joining divisors. When a marked space is the full fiber product of proper relative factors over a smooth simple boundary moduli space, its class is a refined diagonal pullback. For the case of sheaves supported on hyperplane sections of the threefold we discuss construction of the proper relative family by descending the chartwise stable loci, and identify both marked pieces, including the one with zero boundary. To provide some examples, we carry out explicit constructions for the moduli space of surface structure sheaf and its twists. We also prove valuative results for specified sheaves with noninvertible hulls. In a sequel, Part II, we use the construction of degeneration technique in this article to compare quintic invariants with the predicted S-duality modularity of "M5-brane modified elliptic genus" provided by string theorists, Gaiotto Strominger and Yin.
label: arXiv:2611.26207v1

summary.one_liner: We study the specialization of Donaldson-Thomas virtual cycles for surface sheaves on a Calabi Yau threefold degenerating to a simple normal crossing threefold, composed of two quasi Fano threefolds glued along a common (double) divisor.

title: Surface sheaves on the quintic I. Expanded degenerations and virtual gluing

abstract: We prove uniform bounds for the Stein degrees of boundary divisors on generalised log Calabi-Yau fibrations of Fano type over arbitrary fields of characteristic zero. The main ingredient is the birational case for which we provide two approaches.
label: arXiv:2611.25501v1

summary.one_liner: We prove uniform bounds for the Stein degrees of boundary divisors on generalised log Calabi-Yau fibrations of Fano type over arbitrary fields of characteristic zero.

title: Stein degree on birational log Calabi-Yau fibrations

abstract: Persistence diagrams are widely used in topological data analysis to summarize topological and geometric structure in data. We study nonparametric regression where inputs are persistence diagrams and outputs are real-valued. Using kernel-based local averaging estimators defined directly over diagram space with Wasserstein distance, we establish consistency and derive bounds on the rate of convergence under suitable assumptions in the $L^2$-theory. We also present computational experiments that demonstrate strong performance of the proposed estimator, particularly in low data regimes.
label: arXiv:2611.25295v1

summary.background: ['Persistent homology: a method that tracks topological features (connected pieces, loops, voids) across a range of scales, summarized as a persistence diagram.', 'Wasserstein distance: a way to measure how far apart two distributions or point sets are, here applied to two persistence diagrams.', 'Kernel regression: predicting a value by a weighted average of training outputs, where weights fall off with the distance between inputs.', 'Consistency: the property that an estimator converges to the true relationship as the sample size grows.', 'Convergence rate and L² error: how quickly the average squared prediction error shrinks with more data.']
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a kernel-weighted local-averaging regression estimator that takes persistence diagrams as inputs, uses Wasserstein distance as the similarity measure, and proves consistency and convergence-rate bounds in the L² sense.
summary.plain: Data scientists often summarize the shape of a dataset as a 'persistence diagram', a compact list of loops, holes, and clusters that appear at different scales. This paper asks how to predict a single number from such a shape summary, using a method that predicts by averaging the outputs of similar past examples. The authors prove the method gets more accurate as data grows, give a bound on how fast that happens, and report experiments where it performs well, especially with little data. The abstract does not give the details of those experiments.
summary.why: Predicting outcomes from shape features is a practical need in areas like materials science and medical imaging, and this paper gives a theoretical footing for doing so directly in diagram space. The abstract alone does not show how the assumptions or rates compare with other approaches, so the strength of the contribution is hard to judge from it.

title: Kernel Regression using Persistence Diagrams

abstract: We construct a homotopy coherent product structure extending the Chas-Sullivan product on chains of the free loop space of a manifold. Our construction uses the framework of Morse homology with DG coefficients and perturbed Morse gradient trees. We define an operad given by moduli spaces of Morse gradient trees with a twisted differential. This Morse tree operad receives a map from a suspended A$\infty$-operad and in turn acts on Morse homology with DG coefficients associated to a fibration over a manifold with a fibrewise monoidal structure.
label: arXiv:2611.25890v1

summary.one_liner: We construct a homotopy coherent product structure extending the Chas-Sullivan product on chains of the free loop space of a manifold.

title: An A $\infty$ -algebra structure for enriched Morse complexes

abstract: This paper is devoted to study the convergence behavior of the most probable transition paths in a class of multiscale stochastic dynamical systems. First, based on Euler-Lagrange equations, we establish proximity and convergence results in the space of continuous functions endowed with the supremum norm. These results compare the most probable paths of the multiscale system with those of averaged system derived from the averaging principle. Next, we utilize a variational framework and analyze the Onsager-Machlup functionals using $Γ$-convergence. Together with the equi-coercivity of the functional family, we prove the convergence of both their minima and minimizers. Specifically, we show weak convergence of the minimizers in the Cameron-Martin space $H^1$, which implies their strong convergence in $L^2$.
label: arXiv:2611.26205v1

summary.one_liner: This paper is devoted to study the convergence behavior of the most probable transition paths in a class of multiscale stochastic dynamical systems.

title: Convergence of the Most Probable Transition Paths in Multiscale Systems

abstract: Data assimilation (DA) in partially observed nonlinear systems requires repeated estimation of both hidden states and their uncertainty. Conventional nonlinear filtering can be computationally expensive and often relies on an explicit dynamical model. In this paper, we develop the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven dynamical model that maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space, where the dynamics of the latent states follow a conditional Gaussian structure. This structure allows closed-form DA updates in the latent space, while nonlinear encoder-decoder mappings retain the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamics in physical space. A key feature of Neural CGM is its treatment of uncertainty in DA. The latent posterior mean and covariance are mapped to the physical variables through a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections. The resulting physical-space posterior statistics depend on the sequentially updated latent distribution rather than on a separate post-processing estimate. The same statistics enter a Gaussian negative log-likelihood during training, so both the posterior mean and uncertainty affect the learned model. Because Neural CGM learns the dynamical model itself, it can also be used for state forecasting and simulation without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost relative to conventional nonlinear DA methods. Neural CGM is therefore suited to repeated state estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction from partial observations.
label: arXiv:2611.26463v1

summary.background: ['Data assimilation: combining a model of a system with incoming observations to estimate its current hidden state.', "Nonlinear filtering: estimating a hidden state over time when the system's rules are nonlinear, so the uncertainty does not stay simply Gaussian.", 'Gaussian (normal) distribution: a bell-shaped uncertainty described by a mean and a covariance (spread and correlations).', 'Conditional Gaussian structure: a model where some variables are Gaussian once others are known, which allows exact, cheap calculations.', 'Encoder-decoder network: one neural network maps data into a hidden (latent) space and another maps it back.', 'Negative log-likelihood training: fitting a model by rewarding predictions that assign high probability to the observed data.']
summary.one_liner: The paper learns a neural-network dynamical model that encodes partially observed nonlinear states into a latent space where the dynamics are conditional Gaussian, enabling closed-form data assimilation updates and a Gaussian decoder that propagates uncertainty back to physical variables.
summary.plain: Scientists often want to track the hidden state of a complicated system, such as weather, from noisy and incomplete measurements, and to know how uncertain their estimate is. Standard methods for this can be slow and usually need the exact equations governing the system. The authors train a neural network that translates the system into a simpler hidden representation where the update step can be computed directly, then translates back to the physical quantities together with an uncertainty estimate.
summary.why: Fast, uncertainty-aware state tracking matters in areas such as weather prediction and other data assimilation settings where the governing equations are incomplete. The abstract reports lower online cost and accurate estimation and forecasting on benchmark systems, but I cannot judge from the abstract how general these gains are beyond those benchmarks.

title: Neural Conditional Gaussian Model: Efficient Data Assimilation with Sequential Uncertainty Quantification for Nonlinear Dynamics

abstract: A fundamental result in Ramsey theory due to Alon, Frankl and Lovász gives an exact formula for the $q$-colour Ramsey numbers of matchings in $r$-uniform hypergraphs: if $n\ge\mathsf{AFL}_r(\mathbf{t})=(r-1)\|\mathbf{t}\|_\infty+1+\sum_{j=1}^q(t_j-1)$ then in any $q$-edge-colouring of $K^r_n$ there is some colour $j$ with a matching of size $t_j$. We show that a very weak quasirandomness assumption suffices for this Ramsey property: we can replace $K^r_n$ by any $r$-graph $H$ on at least $\mathsf{AFL}_r(\mathbf{t})+o(n)$ vertices that is a sublinear connector, meaning that it has no balanced $r$-partite holes of linear size. This generalises the result for $r=2$ (ordinary graphs) that we proved previously using a compression algorithm based on Gallai-Edmonds decompositions. This structure theory is unavailable in the hypergraph setting, so we combine two other proof methods, namely (a) simultaneous optimisation in all colours by clustering vertices using fractional cover weights from LP duality, and (b) local-to-global structure via random sampling and Kahn's matching theorem.
label: arXiv:2611.25893v1

title: A very robust Ramsey theorem for hypergraph matchings

abstract: For every strength, we prove the existence of rational designs on spheres, orthogonal and unitary groups, real and complex Grassmannians, and ellipsoids that are defined by positive-definite quadratic forms with rational coefficients and have a rational point. This answers Bannai's Problem for these spaces, solves the problem of Cui--Xia--Xiang on rational spherical $4$-designs on the unit circle, and proves Xiang's conjecture in the stronger form of existence in every dimension. To this end, we introduce the $(G,\mathcal{S})$-Prouhet--Tarry--Escott problem for an abelian group $G$ and a finite set of characters $\mathcal{S}$ and develop its existence and minimality theory. We also prove a general theorem transforming integer-weighted rational designs into equi-weighted designs on distinct rational points. On the unit circle $\mathbb{S}^1$, we determine the minimum sizes of rational spherical designs of strengths $4,5,6,7$ and show that they are respectively $2304,4608,9216,9216$. We also show that the minimum size of a rational spherical $5$-design on $\mathbb{S}^2$ is $192$. We further apply our framework to prove a conjecture of Thuswaldner--Ziegler on sums of distinct units and to answer Mahabaduge's problem on convex equilateral lattice polygons affirmatively.
label: arXiv:2611.25516v1

summary.one_liner: For every strength, we prove the existence of rational designs on spheres, orthogonal and unitary groups, real and complex Grassmannians, and ellipsoids that are defined by positive-definite quadratic forms with rational coefficients and have a rational point.

title: Rational Designs and Prouhet--Tarry--Escott Problems

abstract: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.
label: arXiv:2611.25515v1

summary.background: ['Partial differential equation (PDE): an equation relating a function to its rates of change in several variables, used to model heat, waves, fluid flow and similar physics.', 'Neural network as a function approximator: a model with adjustable weights that is trained to fit data or satisfy equations.', 'Physics-informed neural network (PINN): a network trained by minimizing the residual of the PDE (and boundary/initial conditions) at sample points, so the loss measures how well the physics is satisfied.', 'Loss function: the single number the training algorithm tries to make small.', 'Integral constraint: a condition obtained by integrating the governing equation over a domain, added as an extra term in the loss.', 'Stability estimate: a mathematical bound showing how much the output error can grow relative to the size of the loss, indicating how well the loss controls the error.']
summary.one_liner: The paper derives stability estimates for PINN losses with and without integral constraints on several PDEs, showing that in certain parameter regimes the standard loss gives only weak control over some error components while the integral constraints restore uniform control, and supports this with numerical experiments.
summary.plain: Physics-informed neural networks learn approximate solutions to equations describing physical systems by penalizing mistakes in the equation during training. Some researchers have found that adding extra conditions obtained by summing or integrating the equation over a region helps accuracy, but the reason was not well understood. The authors compare error bounds with and without these integral conditions for several equations, and report that in some parameter settings the usual training loss barely controls certain kinds of error, while the integral conditions restore control; their experiments match this, though the abstract does not give details of the specific equations or error sizes.
summary.why: It offers a mathematical explanation for a practical training trick that people have used in scientific machine learning, which helps decide when the trick is worth adding. Whether the reasoning carries over to other equations or network designs is not stated in the abstract and would need the full paper to judge.

title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?

abstract: We develop fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, derive their reduced dynamics, and analyze their long-time behavior by backward error analysis. We derive the continuous Euler-Lagrange equations, energy balance, and Noether conservation laws, and construct time-indexed discrete Lagrangians using retractions, with the midpoint-Cayley scheme treated explicitly. On their regularity domains, the resulting phase-space maps are symplectic. For left-invariant discrete Lagrangians, they reduce to Lie-Poisson maps that preserve coadjoint orbits and, when $G$ is connected, every Casimir function. A variational error analysis establishes second-order accuracy of the midpoint-Cayley method. We also construct an exactly symplectic, projectable extension on $T^*(\mathbb R\times G)$ whose formal modified Hamiltonian is affine in the momentum conjugate to time and admits symmetry reduction. Under uniform analyticity, coefficient bounds, and domain-containment assumptions, optimal truncation yields exponentially accurate interpolation and near-conservation of the modified extended Hamiltonian over exponentially long intervals. For a connected attitude network on $SO(3)^N$ with damping and uniformly positive, non-increasing coupling weights, we prove local asymptotic stability of the static consensus set for the continuous dynamics and exact preservation of total spatial momentum by the discrete scheme. Numerical experiments on the network and on a time-dependent rigid body on $SO(3)$ illustrate second-order convergence and the extended energy balance.
label: arXiv:2611.25313v1

summary.background: ['Lagrangian mechanics: motion obtained from a least-action principle and the Euler-Lagrange equations.', 'Lie groups: smooth groups of transformations such as rotations SO(3); their tangent and cotangent spaces underlie the dynamics.', 'Symplectic maps: transformations that preserve the geometric area structure of phase space, which in turn controls long-run energy behavior.', "Noether's theorem: each continuous symmetry of the Lagrangian gives a conserved quantity, such as momentum.", 'Variational integrators: discrete-time schemes obtained by discretizing the action rather than the equations of motion.', 'Backward error analysis: interpreting a numerical method as the exact flow of a slightly modified equation to explain long-time accuracy.', 'Consensus dynamics: networked agents whose states are driven toward a common value, here rotations.']
summary.one_liner: The paper builds structure-preserving variational time-stepping schemes for time-dependent Lagrangian systems evolving on Lie groups (such as rotations in SO(3)), proves their symplectic and momentum-preserving properties, gives a second-order error bound for a midpoint-Cayley variant, and analyzes long-time near-conservation via backward error analysis with an extended-phase-space formulation.
summary.plain: Many physical systems, such as spinning bodies or networks of orientations, have states that are rotations rather than ordinary numbers, and their laws can change with time. Computer simulations of these systems tend to drift away from the true behavior over long runs, so the authors design step-by-step computational rules that are derived from the system's variational (least-action) principle so they keep key physical quantities in line. They show the schemes preserve geometric structure and momentum, prove the method is second-order accurate, and argue that energy stays nearly constant over exponentially long times under stated assumptions. Numerical tests on a rotating rigid body and a rotation network are reported to match these predictions.
summary.why: Geometry-preserving integrators matter for long simulations in robotics, spacecraft attitude control, and multi-agent synchronization, where drift can accumulate into wrong answers. The paper's combination of time-dependence, Lie-group structure, and consensus stability may interest researchers in geometric numerical integration and control, though the practical reach beyond the stated assumptions is not established by the abstract.

title: Variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups

abstract: This contribution focuses on bisimulation invariance as the hallmark of modal model theory and of modal modelling. It exemplifies traditional as well as more recent ramifications \&\ extensions of classical results -- involving variant modes of bisimulation equivalence and matching modalities also beyond plain Kripke structures, and emphasising especially the technical challenges in finite model theory and other non-elementary settings. Main results to be discussed revolve about the theme of expressive completeness phenomena: beside expressive completeness under bisimulation invariance in relation to first-order background logics, in the style of van Benthem--Rosen characterisations, this also concerns maximality results under criteria form abstract model theory, in the style of Lindstroem theorems.
label: arXiv:2611.26244v1

summary.one_liner: This contribution focuses on bisimulation invariance as the hallmark of modal model theory and of modal modelling.

title: Invariance and Expressiveness: Modal Variations

abstract: This paper introduces a proof format and proof checker for certifying reachability computations of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with polynomial vector fields. Establishing a proof checking framework for certifying ODE reachability is similar to the checking of UNSAT proofs for propositional satisfiability solving, but it is even more important due to the challenges inherent in dealing with ODEs, and even more challenging due to the numerical nature of ODE reachability algorithms. The proofs are expressed in differential dynamic logic (dL), and can be independently verified with symbolic theorem provers for dL (e.g. KeYmaeraX). Such proofs are naturally generated by reachability algorithms based on Taylor models, a popular technique to obtain rigorous bounds on approximations of ODEs. This paper proves the completeness of such proofs - if an approximation was correctly computed by some (possibly untrusted) reachability algorithm via Taylor models, then a corresponding proof in dL can be automatically generated and checked to be correct in dL's proof calculus. A dedicated proof checker is implemented in Lean4 for improved performance, which is capable of formally verifying benchmarks in the ARCH competition.
label: arXiv:2611.25303v1

summary.background: ['Ordinary differential equations (ODEs): equations describing how quantities change continuously over time.', 'Reachability: determining the set of states a system can reach from given starting conditions.', 'Taylor models: a way of representing a function as a polynomial plus a rigorous error bound, used to get guaranteed enclosures of ODE solutions.', 'Differential dynamic logic (dL): a logic for stating and proving properties of hybrid and continuous systems, supported by the KeYmaera X theorem prover.', 'Proof certificates: a result checked by a small trusted program, so the complex solver need not be trusted.', 'Lean4: a proof assistant used here to implement the checker with formal guarantees.', 'Completeness of a proof format: the guarantee that every correct computation has a corresponding checkable proof.']
summary.one_liner: The paper defines a proof format and a Lean4-based proof checker that certify Taylor-model reachability bounds for polynomial ODEs as proofs in differential dynamic logic (dL), and proves that such proofs can always be generated when the underlying approximation is correct.
summary.plain: Computer programs that predict where a system governed by continuous-change equations (like a moving robot or a physical process) will end up often give numerical answers that could be wrong by rounding or approximation errors. This paper asks how to independently check those answers: the authors design a format for writing down a formal proof of each predicted range, and a checker that verifies the proof with a computer proof assistant. They prove that whenever the original approximation was correct, a matching proof of this kind can be produced and checked. The checker is reported to verify benchmark problems from the ARCH competition, though the abstract gives few details beyond that.
summary.why: Trusting numerical tools for safety-critical claims is a real problem, and this work tries to close the gap by making their outputs independently checkable, similar to how SAT solvers' unsatisfiability answers are certified. The connection to formal verification of cyber-physical systems is clear, but the abstract does not indicate how broadly the approach scales beyond the benchmarks.

title: Proof Checking Continuous Reachability

abstract: The one-loop dilatation operator of a superconformal planar gauge theory can be written as a sum of local generators. The algebra these generators satisfy is a powerful organising principle for the spectrum. For SU(2)-like bosonic subsectors we show that this algebra can be read off directly from Feynman diagrams, which we identify as a natural graphical language for it. For N=4 super Yang-Mills this simply reproduces the Temperley-Lieb (TL) algebra of the XXX spin chain. After orbifolding and marginally deforming to N=2 superconformal quiver theories, the same recipe yields dynamical generalisations of the TL algebra. In these theories, the faces of the diagrams are coloured according to the quiver nodes, and separated by domain walls corresponding to bifundamental fields. There are two inequivalent SU(2)-like subsectors, which lead to two different TL algebras. One sector is built from the two bifundamental scalars and (in the simplest case) gives a dynamical TL algebra with a colour-dependent loop fugacity in its quadratic relation. The other sector is built from one bifundamental and one adjoint scalar, and (always) gives a novel algebra, in which the cubic TL relation becomes dynamical. In this latter case, we show that each generator of this new algebra is related to a standard XXZ TL generator by a colour-dependent twist. This twist is local and not an algebra homomorphism, and can be written as a dynamical Drinfeld twist. In both sectors, the TL structure provides a natural graphical approach to the spectral problem, as well as clarifying the structure of the irreducible representations of these chains. Finally, we give a preliminary description of the loop models associated to these algebras.
label: arXiv:2611.26285v1

summary.one_liner: The one-loop dilatation operator of a superconformal planar gauge theory can be written as a sum of local generators.

title: Dynamical Temperley-Lieb algebras from Quiver CFTs

abstract: We construct twists of spinning particles in the classical BV formalism by giving constant backgrounds to the bosonic ghosts of local worldline supersymmetry, in analogy with Costello and Li's twist of supergravity, which gives a nonzero background to the ghost of local spacetime supersymmetry. We represent the superghosts on polynomial states and gauge selected worldline R symmetries, imposing the shifted R constraints absolutely and the unshifted ones relatively. On flat targets, the N=2 particle, its N=4 extension on a complex target and an N=8 particle with two fermion flavors give the de Rham, Dolbeault and polynomial linear BCOV complexes. The last two are the linearized field content of the open and closed B-model target-space theories. Pairings and interactions require target-space input beyond the reduced worldline differentials.
label: arXiv:2611.26554v1

summary.one_liner: We construct twists of spinning particles in the classical BV formalism by giving constant backgrounds to the bosonic ghosts of local worldline supersymmetry, in analogy with Costello and Li's twist of supergravity, which gives a nonzero background to the ghost of local spacetime supersymmetry.

title: Twisting Spinning Particles with Superghost Backgrounds

abstract: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in the FrontierOR benchmark's one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi, with an objective within 1% of Gurobi's and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances. The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark, with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software, within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.
label: arXiv:2611.26171v1

summary.one_liner: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale.

title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research

abstract: We develop a Hamiltonian potential optimization method for partially observed stochastic optimal control with continuous-time state dynamics and discrete-time noisy observations, including controlled sensing. Rather than solving the infinite-dimensional belief-space Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, we optimize over parametrized potentials depending on the state variable and the available observation history. The associated Hamiltonian minimizers induce admissible continuous controls and, when observations are controlled, sensing decisions. An extended Hamiltonian incorporating a cost multiplier provides a common representation of the induced belief dynamics and running and observation costs. This construction yields a finite-dimensional optimization problem, with gradients computed by a forward simulation and a backward discrete adjoint sweep. The numerical implementation uses Gaussian beliefs represented by conditional means and covariances. For nonsmooth Hamiltonians arising from switching controls, we introduce smooth Hamiltonian approximations to enable gradient-based optimization. To assess the resulting policies, we develop belief-space information relaxation lower bounds. A separate optimization of the dual test functional provides a lower bound which, paired with the admissible policy cost, yields an a posteriori primal-dual diagnostic. Numerical experiments investigate scalar and multidimensional linear-quadratic-Gaussian problems, controlled sensing with and without control bounds, a nonquadratic obstacle penalty, and Hamiltonian smoothing for a discontinuous control selector.
label: arXiv:2611.26295v1

summary.background: ['Stochastic optimal control: choosing actions over time to minimize expected cost when the system is driven by random noise.', 'Partial observation: the controller sees only noisy measurements, so it must track a belief (a probability distribution) over the hidden state.', 'Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation: the partial differential equation whose solution gives optimal cost; in belief space it is infinite-dimensional and generally unsolvable directly.', 'Hamiltonian: a function combining cost and dynamics whose minimizer gives the control action at each moment.', 'Linear-quadratic-Gaussian (LQG) problems: linear dynamics, quadratic costs and Gaussian noise, a standard benchmark with known solutions.', 'Gaussian belief: a belief summarized by a mean and covariance, as in Kalman filtering.', 'Adjoint method: a backward sweep that computes gradients of a cost with respect to parameters efficiently.', 'Information relaxation: a technique that gives lower bounds on optimal cost by relaxing the requirement that decisions depend only on available information, plus a penalty term.', 'Primal-dual gap: the difference between an achievable policy cost (primal) and a lower bound (dual) certifies how suboptimal the policy can be.']
summary.one_liner: The paper replaces the infinite-dimensional belief-space HJB equation for partially observed continuous-time control with a finite-dimensional optimization over parametrized Hamiltonian potentials, uses Gaussian belief updates with adjoint gradients, smooths switching-control Hamiltonians, and certifies policies with a primal-dual information-relaxation bound.
summary.plain: Controlling a system when you can only see noisy, partial measurements of it is hard, because the controller must reason about its own uncertainty as well as the system's state. The authors propose a way to design controllers by tuning a small set of adjustable functions of the current state and past measurements, rather than solving an intractable equation over all possible beliefs. They test this on standard textbook-style problems, including cases where the controller also chooses when to take measurements, and pair each policy with a computed lower bound so its quality can be checked.
summary.why: The approach trades an intractable exact formulation for a finite, gradient-trainable one, and the primal-dual bound gives a way to judge how close a policy is to optimal. Its relevance to wider practice depends on how well the numerical experiments, which the abstract describes only at a high level, hold up on harder problems; I am not sure how it compares with existing approximate methods.

title: Hamiltonian Potential Optimization for Partially Observed Stochastic Optimal Control

abstract: We study estimation of the mean latent composition in a bivariate Poisson mixture. Conditional on an unobserved intensity S and proportion U, two counts are independent Poisson variables with respective means SU and S(1-U). The mixing law is unrestricted on the Cartesian product [a,b] x [0,1], where a and b are finite constants satisfying 0 < a < b, and dependence between S and U is allowed. Although the mixing distribution is identifiable, the usual ratio of mean counts estimates an intensity-weighted proportion and may be biased for theta = E[U]. We construct polynomial estimators based on factorial moments and establish the exact leading exponent of the minimax squared-error risk on the logarithmic scale, without claiming an exact multiplicative minimax constant. We also derive the sharp logarithmic separation exponent for testing zero latent covariance and construct an adaptive estimator achieving parametric squared-error risk on the zero-covariance submodel while retaining the optimal full-model logarithmic minimax exponent. Simulations illustrate the bias-variance trade-off, the role of polynomial regularization, and the distinction between theoretically guaranteed and empirically calibrated adaptation.
label: arXiv:2611.26047v1

summary.one_liner: We study estimation of the mean latent composition in a bivariate Poisson mixture.

title: Sharp minimax rates and adaptive estimation of latent proportions in bivariate Poisson mixtures

abstract: Mediation analysis plays an important role in psychology, epidemiology, and genomics. Al- though high-dimensional mediation has been studied extensively, existing inferential methods typically rely on sparsity assumptions that may be difficult to justify when many individually weak mediators collectively produce a substantial effect. We study inference for both the over- all indirect effect and the effect transmitted through an individual mediator in a proportional high-dimensional regime, where the number of mediators and the sample size grow at compa- rable rates, without imposing sparsity on the mediator effects. Standard debiasing procedures for high-dimensional inference commonly rely on design-covariance information or additional structural assumptions on precision-matrix directions. In mediation models, however, the full outcome-design covariance depends on unknown mediator-model coefficients, creating an addi- tional challenge when such information or structure is unavailable. To address this challenge, we introduce an approximate debiasing procedure based on partial ridge regression and show that the resulting estimator is asymptotically bias-corrected and Gaussian. We also develop a cross-fitted estimator with a smaller asymptotic variance than its sample-split counterpart. In addition, we construct consistent estimators of the limiting variances of both the sample-split and cross-fitted estimators. Together, these results provide feasible inferential procedures for global and pathwise mediation effects.
label: arXiv:2611.25864v1

summary.one_liner: Mediation analysis plays an important role in psychology, epidemiology, and genomics.

title: Inference in High-Dimensional Linear Mediation Models

abstract: Synthetic data has emerged as a powerful tool for data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twin development, with growing applications in biomedical research and drug development. However, limited attention has been devoted to synthetic time-to-event data, which are central to clinical trials and survival analysis. In particular, theoretical guarantees for the distributional fidelity of synthetic survival data remain largely unexplored. More importantly, even when a generator achieves distributional fidelity, it remains unclear whether the downstream statistical analysis is reliable. To address these gaps, we propose a general two-stage generative framework for survival data (TSGSurv) that jointly generates observed times and covariates conditional on event status, and establish its distributional convergence rate. Focusing on the widely used Cox proportional hazards model, we establish conditions under which generator fidelity guarantees consistency of model coefficient estimates. We further characterize the limitations of naive inference based on synthetic data, and develop a variance correction and a distribution calibration procedure to recover valid inference of original data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed generative and inferential framework with extensive simulations and two real data applications.
label: arXiv:2611.25464v1

summary.one_liner: Synthetic data has emerged as a powerful tool for data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twin development, with growing applications in biomedical research and drug development.

title: Faithful Generative Modeling for Censored Time-to-Event Data: From Distributional Fidelity to Statistical Inference

abstract: Bayesian neural networks provide principled uncertainty estimates, but training them with Monte Carlo sampling can be expensive. Sampling-free variational inference algorithms make training Bayesian neural networks feasible, but existing approaches assume a Gaussian output distribution, which can be inaccurate in applied problems. Here, we introduce CF-Prop, an uncertainty propagation method that uses characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, without any sampling, even in non-Gaussian settings. Because CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions, the evidence lower bound---the objective of variational training---can be computed in closed form for a broad class of likelihoods, including the Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma. This allows to implement an efficient resulting variational inference algorithm, CF-VI. On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error of any tested method, improving on the next best method by about 35%. On a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset, CF-VI accurately captures tail uncertainty that is severely underestimated by both other sampling-free methods and Monte Carlo methods.
label: arXiv:2611.26426v1

summary.background: ['Bayesian neural network: a network whose weights are probability distributions rather than fixed numbers, so predictions come with uncertainty.', 'Variational inference: training by fitting a simpler distribution to the true posterior, by maximising a score called the evidence lower bound (ELBO).', 'Monte Carlo sampling: estimating quantities by averaging many random draws; accurate but costly.', 'ReLU layer: a standard network layer that outputs the positive part of its input (zero otherwise).', 'Characteristic function: a transform that fully describes a probability distribution, similar in spirit to a Fourier transform.', 'Likelihood: the assumed distribution of observed outcomes given the model, here Gaussian, Poisson or Gamma.', "Calibration error: how far a model's stated confidence is from how often it is actually right."]
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces CF-Prop, a sampling-free way to propagate uncertainty through a Bayesian ReLU layer by working with characteristic functions, which lets the variational training objective be computed in closed form for non-Gaussian likelihoods and yields the CF-VI training algorithm.
summary.plain: Neural networks can be built to report how unsure they are, but the usual way of estimating that uncertainty relies on repeatedly running random samples, which is slow. Earlier fast methods assumed the output uncertainty follows a bell-shaped (Gaussian) curve, which can be wrong for real problems. The authors use a mathematical transform, the characteristic function, to track the exact shape of the output uncertainty without sampling, and they report that this gives better calibration on CIFAR-100 and better tail estimates on a heavy-tailed insurance claims dataset.
summary.why: It targets a practical gap: fast uncertainty estimates that do not assume the output is bell-shaped, which matters for skewed or heavy-tailed data such as insurance losses. The abstract reports the results but not the full experimental details, so the size and generality of the gains are best checked in the full paper; the link to other fields is mainly through risk modelling and calibrated prediction.

title: Exact Bayesian layers via characteristic functions

abstract: Automated ICAO/ISO face-image compliance analysers provide criterion-level pass/fail decisions, yet these verdicts do not quantify uncertainty when deciding whether to accept, reject, or retake a photograph. We investigate conformal prediction as a triage layer for BioGaze, evaluating 14 compliance criteria on the synthetic TONO benchmark. Without retraining the analyser, we fit per-criterion logistic classifiers and compare marginal and label-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction with conventional abstention rules using subject-disjoint splits. Marginal conformal prediction achieved approximately 0.90 overall coverage but substantially under-covered violations, with a ten-partition mean of 0.37 for one criterion. The corresponding Mondrian means ranged from 0.89 to 0.92 across criteria. However, most of the reduction in criterion-level false positives came from the logistic layer (0.145 to 0.048), while tuned abstention rules achieved lower false-positive rates than Mondrian at comparable retake rates. Bonferroni correction for joint coverage across 14 criteria required retaking nearly all images. These findings show that class-conditional conformal prediction can achieve near-target empirical coverage for minority violation classes and reveal trade-offs between statistical coverage, classification performance, and retake requirements in multi-criterion face-image compliance assessment.
label: arXiv:2611.25342v1

summary.one_liner: Automated ICAO/ISO face-image compliance analysers provide criterion-level pass/fail decisions, yet these verdicts do not quantify uncertainty when deciding whether to accept, reject, or retake a photograph.

title: Class-Conditional Conformal Triage for ICAO Face-Image Compliance under Class Imbalance

abstract: The concentration and training-time constancy of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) depend on the interplay between network width, depth, and initialization. While joint depth-width scaling has been studied in fully-connected, residual, and recurrent networks, its effects in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remain less understood. We investigate these effects numerically in CNNs, examining NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training. Let depth $L$ be the number of convolutional layers, and width $C$ the number of channels per layer. We find that NTK dispersion increases with $L/C$ in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes, but remains small in the ordered regime. At critical initialization, dispersion curves approximately collapse as a function of $L/C$, suggesting a nontrivial joint scaling regime. During training, kernel rotation generally increases with $L/C$, even in the ordered regime where initial dispersion is small. Together, these results suggest that $L/C$ may govern NTK deviations from the infinite-width limit in certain regimes, and that NTK concentration at initialization and stability during training exhibit different scaling behaviors.
label: arXiv:2611.25624v1

summary.one_liner: The concentration and training-time constancy of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) depend on the interplay between network width, depth, and initialization.

title: Deviations from the NTK Regime in CNNs under Joint Depth-Width Scaling

abstract: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency.
