Accelerating translation while preserving quality is therefore essential for practical deployment. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate tokens at arbitrary target positions through iterative denoising, offering a new paradigm for parallel translation beyond sequential autoregressive decoding. However, existing methods still incur redundant computation: fixed target generation lengths waste computation on unused positions, while confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have largely stabilized. To address these issues, we propose TRAC, a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation. TRAC adapts the target generation length using source length and translation direction, with a conservative fallback to the maximum length for empty or unusually short outputs. It preserves high-confidence commitment while identifying temporally stable medium-confidence tokens for early commitment using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-$K$ distributions. On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves sentence-level generation speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over Fast-dLLM, with only a 0.02-point decrease in macro-average COMET. These results demonstrate that adaptive generation lengths and stability-aware token commitment improve the efficiency of diffusion machine translation.
label: arXiv:2611.25643v1

summary.one_liner: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency.

title: TRAC: Efficient Diffusion Language Models for Machine Translation via Length-Aware Decoding

abstract: Prosodic prominence can largely be predicted from the words of a sentence, but part of it depends on how the speaker reads it. We study how much of prominence language models recover from text, whether they can report it when asked, and what the speech signal adds. On read English speech labelled for word-level prominence, we compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted large language models (LLMs) and speech models on the same words. All text models end within about one point of each other, at best 68.8% on the 3-way task, and largely make the same errors. With the prompts we tested, LLMs do no better than a word-majority baseline, even with 500 examples. Linear probes find more in their representations. Speech models reach 84.7%. We argue that text determines only part of prominence, and that the rest has to be heard. LLMs encode what the text determines, but prompting does not bring it out: they represent more about where the emphasis falls than they tell you.
label: arXiv:2611.25808v1

summary.background: ['Prosodic prominence: the perceived emphasis on a word in speech, shown through pitch, loudness and length.', 'Three-way task: labelling each word into one of three prominence classes; 68.8% is the best text-model accuracy reported.', 'Word-majority baseline: always guessing the most common label for each word, a simple reference point.', 'Frozen vs. fine-tuned models: frozen models keep their original weights; fine-tuned models have been further trained on the task.', 'Prompting: asking a model a question in natural language, without changing its weights.', "Linear probe: a simple linear classifier trained on a model's internal activations to test what information they contain.", 'Representation vs. report: a model can encode information internally without it appearing in its answers.']
summary.one_liner: The paper tests how much word-level prominence (which word is emphasized in speech) can be recovered from text alone by frozen or fine-tuned text models, prompted LLMs, and speech models, and finds that LLM representations hold more of this information than prompting elicits.
summary.plain: When people speak, some words get more emphasis than others, and this depends partly on the words and partly on how the speaker chooses to read them. The authors asked how much of this emphasis a language model can work out from written text, whether it can say so when asked, and how much extra a recording of speech adds. Text models and prompted chatbots did about as well as a simple 'pick the usually-stressed word' baseline, while a linear probe (a small readout trained on the model's internal numbers) found more, and speech models did best.
summary.why: It shows a gap between what a model's internal representations contain and what it reports when prompted, which matters for anyone relying on prompting to read out model knowledge. The abstract does not say how far the finding extends beyond this task, so its wider significance is uncertain.

title: Language models represent more about emphasis than they can tell you

abstract: Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual monitoring by operators introduces human error and operational inefficiency. This research developed and evaluated an automated gauge reading system using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Three hybrid approaches were implemented and compared: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer vision), OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with VGG19 (deep learning approaches). A comprehensive dataset of 1,848 pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR range) was curated through web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation techniques. The experimental results demonstrate that ResNet18 significantly outperforms the alternatives, achieving an accuracy of 97.3%, compared to VGG19's 64.4% and Scikit-Image's 63.8%. The study validates the effectiveness of residual learning architectures for industrial gauge digitization, providing a robust foundation for Industry 5.0 automation applications.
label: arXiv:2611.26262v1

summary.one_liner: Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual monitoring by operators introduces human error and operational inefficiency.

title: Digitization of Analogue Gauges using Computer Vision

abstract: Flow matching enables high-quality image and video generation, but its iterative sampling process requires repeated evaluations of large neural networks. Existing few-step methods can distort the output and reduce its agreement with a many-step reference. We propose TrajCal, a training-free calibration framework for few-step sampling. Based on scatter search, a well-established metaheuristic for difficult optimization problems, TrajCal starts with diverse seed schedules, deforms and combines these candidates, and selects one fixed schedule by final output fidelity for reuse on new inputs. For both image and video generation, TrajCal achieves higher reference fidelity than all compared baselines at low evaluation budgets while maintaining competitive visual quality. The search is effective even with randomly generated seeds, while trajectory-based seeds further improve fidelity. For cross-style generalization, photography-calibrated schedules also improve fidelity on unseen image styles.
label: arXiv:2611.25847v1

summary.background: ['Flow matching: a generative method that turns noise into an image by following a learned velocity field over a sequence of steps.', 'Sampling steps and schedules: the number and timing of steps set the trade-off between speed and output quality; a schedule is the list of those timings.', 'Few-step sampling: generating with far fewer network evaluations than the standard many-step process, which can introduce errors.', 'Reference fidelity: how closely a fast output matches the output of a slow many-step reference run on the same input.', 'Scatter search: a population-based metaheuristic that combines and modifies candidate solutions to explore hard optimization problems.', 'Training-free: the method adjusts how sampling is done and does not retrain the generative model.']
summary.one_liner: TrajCal is a training-free method that uses scatter search to find one fixed timestep schedule for few-step flow-matching samplers, selected by how closely the few-step output matches a many-step reference, and reuses it across new inputs and image styles.
summary.plain: Modern image and video generators build their output through many small refinement steps, and each step runs a large neural network, which is slow. Faster versions take fewer steps but can distort the result compared with the slow, full version. The authors propose TrajCal, which searches for a good fixed schedule of step timings, scored by how well the quick output matches the slow reference, and reports better agreement at low step budgets while keeping visual quality competitive.
summary.why: Cutting the cost of generation without retraining the model is a practical goal for image and video tools. The abstract does not give the baselines, metrics, or budgets in detail, so its scale of gain is hard to judge from this text alone; the method may also be relevant to other few-step samplers, but the abstract does not claim that.

title: TrajCal: Trajectory-Calibrated Time Schedules for Few-Step Flow Sampling

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.
label: arXiv:2611.25597v1

summary.background: ['Post-training of LLMs: fine-tuning a pretrained model with supervised examples and then with reinforcement learning.', 'Reinforcement learning basics: a policy is updated to increase expected reward, often via policy gradients.', 'Predict-then-optimize: a model forecasts parameters, which feed a downstream optimization problem that chooses a decision.', 'Decision regret: the extra cost of a decision made from a forecast compared with the decision made with perfect information.', 'Prediction loss versus decision cost: a forecast can have low error yet still produce a costly decision.', 'Reward approximation: exact reward evaluation requires solving the optimization problem, which can be expensive, so cheaper estimates are used.']
summary.one_liner: The paper post-trains LLMs to produce optimization parameters by using negative downstream decision regret as the RL reward, with two reward-cost reduction schemes (heuristic warm-starting and randomized reward correction) for when exact evaluation is expensive.
summary.plain: An AI model that forecasts things, like demand, is usually trained to be accurate, but a forecast that is accurate on average can still lead to poor decisions when someone plans around it. The authors train a language model to make forecasts judged by the cost of the decisions they lead to, using a reward signal that penalizes extra cost compared with the best possible decision. On three synthetic problems and a knapsack task, they report gains over methods trained only on prediction error; on an inventory planning task using H&M sales and product descriptions, they report regret reductions of 31.4% versus a supervised fine-tuning baseline and 12.4% versus the strongest conventional forecasting baseline they tested.
summary.why: It targets the gap between prediction accuracy and decision quality, a theme in the 'predict-then-optimize' literature, and applies it to LLM post-training, where text context is used for forecasts. The abstract does not show how far the results generalize beyond the tested tasks, so the broader significance is uncertain.

title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training

abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.
label: arXiv:2611.25742v1

summary.one_liner: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons.

title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models

abstract: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency. However, reinforcing them with black-box rewards, as is routine for multi-step models, faces two structural challenges. First, a few-step generator is a sampler rather than a score model, so its velocity is not the forward velocity of the generated distribution. Second, it must be anchored to the undistilled teacher, which shares no transitions with it. Existing few-step RL methods handle the latter with a marginal KL to the teacher, but each pays for the former in its reward credit. We propose Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), which renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and obtains the credit from their shadow posterior. From the KL-regularized reward objective, we derive a regression loss that turns reward values into a reward direction while anchoring the generator's outputs to the teacher and aligning the shadow inputs with the deployed inputs. Applied to 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step RL methods.
label: arXiv:2611.25998v1

summary.one_liner: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency.

title: Reinforcing Few-Step Diffusion Models via Shadow Posterior Matching

abstract: "AI safety" has grown from a niche contingent of actors into the dominant framing for artificial intelligence (AI) assessment and evaluation, overshadowing AI ethics. Through political and monetary influence, AI safety has shifted political focus within the US and abroad. The focus has shifted away from harms that currently affect the public toward threats framed as "existential risks". We argue that safety cannot be achieved while anti-Blackness is left unaddressed. We ground this argument in Sylvia Wynter's critique of the "overrepresentation" of Man: the modern, Western conception of the Human that is predicated on the subjugation and othering of Blackness. To analyze the state of addressing anti-Blackness in the age of AI safety, we conduct a two-stage, language model-assisted content analysis of 69,290 accepted main-track papers from ten leading machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), and AI ethics conferences (2020--2025). Safety research grew from 0.5% of accepted papers in 2020 to 6.4% in 2025, overtaking ethics. Yet 94% of safety papers rely on automated metrics, and only 11% of safety papers mention harms that affect society directly, compared with 78% of ethics papers. Of the 2,182 safety papers, 8 mention race; none make it central, and none name Black or African-diaspora communities. Across all 254 identified as race-focused papers, only 3 describe racial harm in safety terms, and 55% appear at three ethics venues that publish 2.5% of the corpus. We offer this interdisciplinary examination of AI safety to argue that a just technological future depends on confronting anti-Blackness directly.
label: arXiv:2611.25302v1

summary.one_liner: "AI safety" has grown from a niche contingent of actors into the dominant framing for artificial intelligence (AI) assessment and evaluation, overshadowing AI ethics.

title: Whose Safety? Addressing Anti-Blackness in the Age of AI Safety

abstract: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies. Deep Hedging leverages neural networks to learn flexible hedging policies but relies on opaque models and typically requires large training datasets, which can complicate interpretation and limit its effectiveness in data-constrained settings. X Hedging takes a step toward addressing these limitations by replacing neural networks with tree ensemble methods, specifically LightGBM, to estimate hedging strategies. This design provides a computationally efficient alternative while preserving strong hedging performance and moving toward more user-centered explainability. To integrate LightGBM into a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework, we introduce an optimization approach that sequentially trains tree-ensemble models while introducing stochasticity through random training orders. In controlled experiments, X Hedging achieves performance comparable to Deep Hedging while offering greater user-centered explainability, improved computational efficiency, and substantially higher robustness when training data are limited. The numerical results demonstrate that tree-ensemble methods provide an effective computational alternative to neural networks for data-driven dynamic hedging.
label: arXiv:2611.25870v1

summary.one_liner: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies.

title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework

abstract: Machine learning (ML) is now a standard tool for forecasting the output of solar photovoltaic (PV) plants, yet published accuracy figures are often hard to compare and harder to trust. Many studies validate with random splits, report no reference forecast, and present feature attributions without saying what they can and cannot show. This paper reviews the main families of ML methods for PV power forecasting and resource assessment, from tree ensembles to deep and foundation models, and sets out a reproducible workflow that combines automated model search with explainable AI. The workflow is then tested on an openly available dataset: a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto, Portugal, forecast one day ahead from a 4 km numerical weather prediction grid. Over a full test year, the best models reach a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) of 11.6% of installed capacity, about half the error of smart persistence. The choice of input features changed accuracy far more than the choice among strong algorithms, and shuffled cross-validation was mildly optimistic. After conformal calibration, the nominal 80% prediction intervals covered 81.7% of observations, against 64.5% before. SHAP rankings stayed stable when the model was retrained on different periods but shifted when correlated inputs were removed, so attributions should be read as properties of a model rather than of the plant. The paper closes with practical lessons and open problems, including deployment on edge hardware and the effect of a changing climate.
label: arXiv:2611.25894v1

summary.one_liner: Machine learning (ML) is now a standard tool for forecasting the output of solar photovoltaic (PV) plants, yet published accuracy figures are often hard to compare and harder to trust.

title: Explainable AI for Solar PV Power Forecasting: From Model Selection to Trustworthy, Reproducible Deployment

abstract: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time. This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model's test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term. Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower performance when additional inference compute is available.
label: arXiv:2611.26172v1

summary.one_liner: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time.

title: Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy

abstract: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.
label: arXiv:2611.25763v1

summary.one_liner: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding.

title: Closing Performance Gap for Diffusion Language Models under Low Inference Budgets

abstract: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.
label: arXiv:2611.25980v1

summary.one_liner: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world.

title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models

abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at https://alwaysleepy.github.io/MoRE-WM-site/.
label: arXiv:2611.25336v1

summary.background: ['World model: a learned model that predicts how the environment will change after an action, used by robots to imagine outcomes before acting.', "Mixture of experts: a neural network design where a gating mechanism routes inputs to specialized sub-networks ('experts') rather than using one network for everything.", 'Rigid vs. deformable dynamics: rigid objects keep their shape when pushed, while deformable ones (cloth, dough, rope) bend and change shape, which needs different modeling.', "Prehensile manipulation: actions where the robot grasps and holds an object, so the object's motion is tied to the gripper.", 'Model Predictive Control (MPC): a planning method that repeatedly simulates candidate action sequences with a model, picks the best one, executes the first step, and replans.', 'Sim-to-real data: training on a mix of simulated and real-world recordings to cover more cases than real data alone provides.']
summary.one_liner: MoRE is a 3D world model for robots that uses a mixture of motion experts, one each for rigid, deformable, and prehensile (grasping) dynamics, and plugs into model predictive control for manipulation.
summary.plain: A robot that plans its moves needs a model of how objects will move in response to its actions, but objects behave very differently: a rigid block, a squishy cloth, and a held object each follow different physics. The authors split these cases into separate 'expert' sub-models inside one network, so each type of motion gets its own specialized treatment. They report that this improves prediction accuracy across these regimes and gives better results when the model is used to control a real robot.
summary.why: Robots that must handle many kinds of objects need predictive models that do not blur together different physical behaviors, so this design choice is relevant to manipulation research. The abstract gives only a high-level summary, so the size of the gains and how broadly they hold are unclear without the full paper.

title: MoRE: Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Physics Robotic World Models

abstract: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.
label: arXiv:2611.25663v1

summary.one_liner: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH.

title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition

abstract: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.
label: arXiv:2611.25664v1

summary.one_liner: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal.

title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction

abstract: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Our case study asks how much of their quantitative content can be recovered under the assumption FPT $\neq$ W[1]. The reductions encode the choice of a clique in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of that encoding. This makes a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem yield a fixed-parameter algorithm for deciding whether a graph has a clique of the requested size. We obtain twelve lower bounds for deterministic algorithms across graph, string, and integer feasibility problems, including bounds that hold under structural restrictions. In several cases the same function of the parameter appears in the exponent as in the historical bound, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.
label: arXiv:2611.26080v1

summary.one_liner: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis.

title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]

abstract: Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP is the generalization of the Asymmetric Traveling Salesperson Problem where we are looking for $k$ walks, each with prescribed start $s_i$ and prescribed end $t_i$, such that every vertex is visited by at least one of the walks. The objective is to minimize the total length of all walks. In general, it is NP-hard to find any approximation for this problem in polynomial time (even if the approximation factor is allowed to depend on the number of vertices). We show that one can obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in time $n^{O(k)}$, answering an open question by Friggstad [2013]. For the special case where all tour start vertices $s_i$ are identical and all end vertices $t_i$ are identical, we obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in polynomial time, as well as an $(O(\frac{1}ε), 1+ε)$-bicriteria approximation. For the multi-depot setting, where $s_i =t_i$ for all $i$, we obtain a constant-factor approximation in polynomial time. Finally, our results imply improved constant-factor approximation algorithms for Asymmetric Regret-Bounded Vehicle Routing and unit-weight Path ATSP.
label: arXiv:2611.26188v1

summary.one_liner: Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP is the generalization of the Asymmetric Traveling Salesperson Problem where we are looking for $k$ walks, each with prescribed start $s_i$ and prescribed end $t_i$, such that every vertex is visited by at least one of the walks.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP

abstract: Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.
label: arXiv:2611.26312v1

summary.background: ['Static analyzer: a tool that inspects code without running it and reports suspicious patterns, such as possible security flaws.', 'LLM code generation: a large language model writes program source code from a natural-language request.', 'Iterative repair loop: generate code, run the analyzer, ask the model to fix the reported issues, and repeat, which costs many extra model calls.', 'Rollback: discarding the partially generated output and restarting from the point where the alert appeared.', 'Functional vs. secure: a program can be correct for its task yet still contain a security vulnerability; benchmarks check both with test oracles.', 'Output tokens: the text units a model produces; a common proxy for compute cost.', "False or conflicting alerts: analyzer warnings that do not match the task's actual requirements, which can push the model toward a wrong program."]
summary.one_liner: The paper compares two ways of feeding static-analyzer warnings into an LLM during code generation (as a code comment or in the user message, after rolling back on an alert) against iterative repair loops and a no-analyzer control, measuring functional and secure output on three Python benchmarks.
summary.plain: AI models that write code often produce programs with security holes, and tools that scan code for such problems can point them out. This paper tests a cheaper way to use those scanner reports: when the scanner flags a problem during writing, the model's draft is rolled back and the warning is fed back as a code comment or as part of the user's message. The authors report that this costs roughly 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output, compared with up to 24 times for repeated fix-and-retry loops, and it raised the share of correct, secure programs in one tested setup from 52.5% to 64.4%.
summary.why: Scanner-guided generation is a practical middle ground between no feedback and costly repair loops, and the paper also reports when it backfires, such as when a warning conflicts with the task. Its results come from specific models and benchmarks, so how well they transfer to other settings is an open question.

title: Static Analysis Guidance for Secure LLM Code Generation

abstract: Motivated by the non-standard interpretations of if-then-else in probabilistic and quantum programs we review the different semantics of conditional branching and propose a unifying categorical structure for the interpretation of if-then-else. We show that many semantically important categories possess this structure, covering inter alia classical, probabilistic, quantum or non-deterministic computations. We examine algebraic structures related to and generated by this categorical structure, in particular on collections of predicates. In this setting we show that the skew-associativity rules of GKATs and barycentric algebras are two instances of a common skew-associativity rule.
label: arXiv:2611.26400v1

summary.one_liner: Motivated by the non-standard interpretations of if-then-else in probabilistic and quantum programs we review the different semantics of conditional branching and propose a unifying categorical structure for the interpretation of if-then-else.

title: On the semantics of conditional branching

abstract: Embedded computing demands high performance and energy efficiency across workloads with widely different computational characteristics. Choosing the most suitable execution model therefore requires a quantitative understanding of how each model maps to different workload classes. In this paper, we compare three execution models for energy-efficient embedded computing: scalar multicore, stream ing multicore, and vector processing. We use three open-source RISC-V accelerators as representative implementations: the PULP Cluster, the Snitch Cluster, and Spatz, respectively. Their open-source hardware and software stacks enable a controlled comparison based on implementations in the same 12 nm technology and a common benchmark suite. Our results reveal that no single execution model performs best across all workload classes. Spatz delivers the greatest benefits for regular and highly vectorizable compute-intensive applications, achieving up to 4.29x higher performance and 5.17x greater energy efficiency than the other architectures. However, its effectiveness strongly depends on the availability of data-level parallelism and regular computation and memory-access patterns, making it the most sensitive to workload characteristics. The Snitch Cluster performs particularly well on applications with limited parallelism and streamable memory-access patterns, providing up to 5.53x higher performance and 1.45x greater energy efficiency. Conversely, the PULP Cluster is most effective on irregular and control-dominated applications, achieving improvements of up to 5.66x in performance and 2.80x in energy efficiency. Compared with Spatz, however, the greater flexibility offered by PULP and Snitch comes at a non-negligible cost in terms of both area and power.
label: arXiv:2611.25947v1

summary.one_liner: Embedded computing demands high performance and energy efficiency across workloads with widely different computational characteristics.

title: Matching Architecture to Workload: Comparing RISC-V Parallel Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Embedded Computing

abstract: Improving microprocessor performance while meeting ASIC implementation constraints like area and frequency is a complex and labor-intensive task that requires expertise across computer architecture, hardware design, and performance analysis and profiling. While large teams in industry can afford the engineering resources to target this problem across performance modeling, RTL design, and ASIC implementations, small teams of researchers and engineers cannot take on this huge engineering burden while keeping up with the pace of advancement in processor microarchitecture. Recent advancements in large language model (LLM) agents present a promising substrate to accelerate this traditionally human-intensive process. In this work, we build and evaluate MiracleGro, an agentic AI-based system that, without human intervention, analyzes cycle-level RTL behavior and synthesis results, identifies performance bottlenecks, and translates architectural ideas into RTL implementation in a leading open-source out-of-order superscalar application core, the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). Taking into account cycle-exact performance, area, and critical path, MiracleGro automatically produces improved BOOM designs that drastically increase the human-optimized BOOM's performance on substantial workload suites such as SPEC CPU2017 with full reference inputs. MiracleGro achieves an 85% IPC speedup and a frequency improvement of 27% in SkyWater 130nm, resulting in a 2.34x wall-clock time speedup on the full SPEC CPU2017 intspeed benchmarks (30 trillion instructions). This result demonstrates the enormous opportunity to harness frontier models to improve state-of-the-art RTL-driven platforms for implementation-grounded microarchitecture research across hardware designs.
label: arXiv:2611.26517v1

summary.one_liner: Improving microprocessor performance while meeting ASIC implementation constraints like area and frequency is a complex and labor-intensive task that requires expertise across computer architecture, hardware design, and performance analysis and profiling.

title: From Seed to BLOOM: Autonomously Growing a Better Out-of-Order Core

abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to protect sensitive data in visualization, but understanding how privacy-induced noise affects visual representations remains fragmented. Prior work has examined the impact of DP noise on specific chart types, yet these findings are typically tied to particular chart types and evaluation settings, making it difficult to generalize across contexts. In parallel, visualization research has long established that visual channels, the visual properties of marks that encode data attributes, differ in perceptual effectiveness under noise-free conditions. However, these principles have not been systematically revisited under DP, where noise is deliberately introduced into the data to protect privacy. In this paper, we present a channel-centric perspective to reframe prior empirical and theoretical results. Our synthesis drawson prior findings to motivate a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis: the utility of DP visualizations may depend on the task-relevant reads made salient by visual channel configurations and DP mechanism choice jointly. Moreover, this perspective highlights the role of channel choice throughout the privacy-preserving visualization pipeline, from disclosure framing and DP algorithm design to utility evaluation and interpretation of noisy outputs. The synthesis also identifies gaps in the existing evaluation literature and highlights research opportunities for channel-aware DP visualization.
label: arXiv:2611.26396v1

summary.background: ["Differential privacy (DP): a mathematical guarantee that results reveal little about any single person's record, achieved by adding random noise to data or outputs.", 'Visual channels: the visual properties of marks (position, length, color, size, shape) that encode data values in a chart.', 'Perceptual effectiveness: how accurately and quickly people read values from different channels; some channels are easier to read than others without noise.', 'Utility: how useful a visualization remains for its intended task after privacy noise is added.', 'Task-relevant reads: the specific judgments a viewer needs to make from a chart, such as comparing values or spotting a trend.']
summary.one_liner: This paper reframes existing findings on how differential privacy noise affects charts through the lens of visual channels (position, color, size and similar mark properties), and proposes a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis for when privacy-protected visualizations stay useful.
summary.plain: Differential privacy adds carefully calibrated random noise to data so that individuals cannot be picked out, but the noise can make charts harder to read. The authors argue that earlier studies of this effect were tied to specific chart types, so they look at the problem through 'visual channels', the properties such as position, length or color that encode data values. They synthesize prior work, rather than running new experiments, to suggest that a chart's usefulness under noise depends on both which channels carry the data and which privacy mechanism is used.
summary.why: It offers a common vocabulary for comparing privacy-preserving charts across chart types and points to gaps in how these tools are evaluated, which matters for anyone designing or judging privacy-protected dashboards. Because the paper is a synthesis from the abstract alone, the strength of its hypothesis rests on how well the cited prior studies support it, which I cannot check here.

title: Rethinking Utility in Differentially Private Visualization: A Channel-Centric Perspective

abstract: People often watch videos to find information, but locating relevant moments can be difficult and time-consuming. Existing strategies like scrubbing rely primarily on visual scanning and linear search, providing limited support for goal-directed navigation. We present VideoTrail, an AI-powered browser extension that supports information seeking in videos through a hierarchical visualization. Inspired by information foraging theory, VideoTrail surfaces semantic and structural cues as information scent, creating an explorable roadmap of segments. The system is multimodal and adaptive, prioritizing visual or textual scent based on the video's content. In a user study (N=16), VideoTrail helped participants efficiently locate key moments and enabled new navigation strategies compared to traditional timelines, highlighting how exposing an adaptive video structure can enhance goal-directed viewing.
label: arXiv:2611.25377v1

summary.background: ["Scrubbing: dragging the playhead along a video's progress bar to skip ahead or review.", "Information foraging theory: a model from HCI saying people navigate information by following cues ('scent') that suggest where useful content lies.", 'Hierarchical visualization: showing information as nested levels, such as chapters containing sections, rather than one flat list.', 'Semantic cues: meaning-based signals such as topics or transcript text; structural cues: layout signals such as scene or section boundaries.', 'Multimodal: using more than one type of input, here visual frames and text.', 'Browser extension: a small add-on that adds features to a web browser without changing the video site itself.']
summary.one_liner: VideoTrail is a browser extension that replaces a plain video timeline with an AI-generated hierarchical map of segments, using semantic and structural cues as information scent to support goal-directed video navigation, evaluated in a 16-person user study.
summary.plain: People often have to watch long videos or scrub back and forth along a progress bar to find one specific moment, which is slow and hit-or-miss. VideoTrail is a browser add-on that uses AI to break a video into a nested outline of sections, with cues such as topics and on-screen text, so viewers can head toward the part they want. The authors report that in a study with 16 participants, it helped people find key moments more efficiently than a traditional timeline and allowed new ways of navigating, though the abstract gives no detailed figures.
summary.why: It applies a well-known idea from information foraging theory, where people follow scent cues toward likely targets, to the everyday problem of searching video, which may matter for education, lecture review and tutorial use. The abstract is thin on measured results, so how large or robust the benefit is remains unclear from this summary alone.

title: VideoTrail: Interactive Video Foraging Through Hierarchical Visualization

abstract: Quantum locally recoverable codes with $(r,δ)$-locality ($(r,δ)$-qLRCs) are quantum error-correcting codes in which $δ-1$ erased qudits can be recovered by accessing only $r$ other qudits. The minimum locality of a qLRC is the least $r$ such that it has $(r,δ)$-locality. This paper aims to construct optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets and explicit minimum localities, where the optimality is measured by the Singleton-like bound of Guruswami, Kshirsagar, and Trivedi (GKT-optimal). Such qLRCs have particular advantages in recovering as many quantum erasures as possible while operating in parallel and with minimal qudit access overhead. We first characterize the recovering sets and the minimum locality of any CSS code by local relative distances, which are relative minimum distances of punctured codes with respect to shortened codes. We then construct impure qLRCs as CSS codes from nested pairs of generalized monomial-Cartesian codes. Grouping the monomials by their degree in the last variable, we reduce both their minimum distances and their local recovery to nested pairs of codes in the remaining variables, and the coordinates with the same values of these variables form disjoint recovering sets. In this way, we obtain four infinite families of GKT-optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets, and determine their minimum localities and the recovering sets attaining them for every admissible $δ$, except for a partial range of $δ$ in one family. These minimum localities need not be monotone in $δ$. In particular, two of the families contain GKT-optimal impure subfamilies of CSS codes CSS$(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})$ with $(r,δ)$-locality for some $r<n-δ+1$ at values of $δ$ for which $\mathcal{C}$ has no classical $(r',δ)$-locality for any $0<r'<n$, where $n$ is the length of $\mathcal{C}$.
label: arXiv:2611.25859v1

summary.one_liner: Quantum locally recoverable codes with $(r,δ)$-locality ($(r,δ)$-qLRCs) are quantum error-correcting codes in which $δ-1$ erased qudits can be recovered by accessing only $r$ other qudits.

title: Optimal Impure $(r,δ)$-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes with Explicit Minimum Localities

abstract: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.
label: arXiv:2611.25496v1

summary.one_liner: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference?

title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing

abstract: We study the dynamics of the most general metric teleparallel spacetimes of Bianchi types II, III and IX, which admit a four-dimensional symmetry group, in the 1-parameter family of New General Relativity. We first show that in each of these classes the most general metric teleparallel geometry is described by four free functions of time, while another four functions of time describe the most general energy-momentum tensor compatible with the same symmetries. We then derive the field equations of New General Relativity for this class of geometries. Finally, we present some solutions to these field equations. Our results show that both solutions resembling features of the standard Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker cosmology of General Relativity and deviations thereof exist.
label: arXiv:2611.26474v1

summary.background: ["General relativity: Einstein's theory in which gravity is spacetime curvature, described by the metric (the rule for measuring distances and times).", 'Teleparallel gravity: an equivalent-in-spirit reformulation that uses torsion (a twisting of the geometry) instead of curvature to describe gravity, with the metric as the main variable.', 'New General Relativity: a one-parameter family of teleparallel theories; the parameter selects a specific member of the family.', 'Bianchi models: spatially uniform but possibly anisotropic (direction-dependent) universe models, classified into types such as II, III and IX.', 'Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) cosmology: the standard isotropic, homogeneous model of the expanding universe.', 'Field equations: the differential equations linking geometry to matter content; solving them gives the time evolution of the universe model.']
summary.one_liner: The paper derives and partially solves the field equations of New General Relativity (a one-parameter family of teleparallel gravity theories) for spatially homogeneous Bianchi II, III and IX cosmological models that possess a four-dimensional symmetry group.
summary.plain: Physicists build models of how the universe expands, and the standard model uses Einstein's general relativity, where gravity is curvature of spacetime. This paper works in an alternative formulation, teleparallel gravity, where gravity is described by a different geometric quantity, and it studies a family of such theories called New General Relativity. The authors restrict to simple, highly symmetric universe shapes (Bianchi types II, III and IX) and show that the geometry and the matter content can each be described by a small set of functions of time. They then write down the equations these theories require and present some solutions, which the abstract says include cases resembling the standard expanding-universe model and cases that deviate from it.
summary.why: It tests whether alternative geometric descriptions of gravity can produce cosmologies that look like the standard one or differ from it in checkable ways, which matters for work on dark energy and modified gravity. The abstract does not indicate how the deviations compare with observations, so its relevance to real data is unclear from this summary alone.

title: Bianchi cosmologies with four-dimensional groups of motion in New General Relativity

abstract: We study quantum-gravitational corrections to the planar integrable structure of the symmetric product orbifold $\text{Sym}^N(\mathbb{T}^4)$ that is dual to tensionless string theory on AdS$_3\times$S$^3\times \mathbb{T}^4$. We consider the deformation that switches on R-R flux in the bulk, and analyze the associated level spacing statistics. The leading non-planar corrections lift the planar degeneracies and produce signs of random-matrix behavior. Our results provide a controlled example of string interactions driving the onset of quantum chaos.
label: arXiv:2611.25576v1

summary.one_liner: We study quantum-gravitational corrections to the planar integrable structure of the symmetric product orbifold $\text{Sym}^N(\mathbb{T}^4)$ that is dual to tensionless string theory on AdS$_3\times$S$^3\times \mathbb{T}^4$.

title: From Integrability to Chaos in Tensionless AdS3 String Theory

abstract: As anything not in equilibrium is, by definition, nonequilibrium, there is no universally agreed-upon set of topics that can constitute an exhaustive presentation of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. At the same time, nonequilibrium statistical mechanics has transcended traditional physics to become a powerful language for complex systems. Prompted by an enthusiastic curiosity about complex systems, these cursory lecture notes attempt to elucidate some introductory concepts and techniques used in classical nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, which find successful applications not only in foundational physics, but also across other fields such as biology, ecology, economics, and sociology. Except for the specific synthesis and presentation of the material, which assumes basic familiarity with equilibrium statistical mechanics, the author claims no originality.
label: arXiv:2611.26394v1

summary.background: ['Equilibrium statistical mechanics: how microscopic states give rise to macroscopic quantities like temperature and pressure', 'Basic probability and averages over ensembles of states', 'The general idea of a system being driven away from equilibrium, for example by a temperature or energy gradient', 'Basic calculus and differential equations']
summary.one_liner: These are introductory lecture notes that present core concepts and mathematical techniques of classical nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, assuming prior knowledge of equilibrium statistical mechanics.
summary.plain: Statistical mechanics explains how the behavior of huge collections of particles relates to averages and probabilities, and most of its textbook tools assume the system has settled into equilibrium. These lecture notes gather the basic ideas and mathematical methods for the harder case of systems that are not settled, such as systems driven by flows of energy or matter. The author says the material is a synthesis and presentation of existing ideas, not new results, and notes that the same tools are used in biology, ecology, economics and sociology. The abstract does not state specific findings.
summary.why: It is a teaching resource for readers who want an entry point into nonequilibrium methods used across complex-systems fields; the abstract itself makes no claims of new results, so its value lies in pedagogy rather than discovery. I cannot tell from the abstract which specific cross-field applications the notes cover.

title: Nonequilibrium Statistical Mechanics: Physical Concepts & Mathematical Tools

abstract: Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model, head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical from dynamical origins of head specialization.
label: arXiv:2611.26228v1

summary.one_liner: Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior.

title: Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity

abstract: Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics. We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), which exploit the locally-entangled subspace of Gaussian states to give an architecture more compatible with modern neural networks and an exact contraction cost of $O(N^{3/2})$ on two-dimensional lattices. For the Hubbard model at $U/t=8$ and $1/8$ hole doping, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies in large lattices of up to 1024 sites. These results demonstrate an accurate approach to strongly correlated fermions by connecting neural networks with Gaussian tensor networks.
label: arXiv:2611.26604v1

summary.one_liner: Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics.

title: Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Fermions with Neural Gaussian Tensor Networks

abstract: The scaling of multi-element quantized Hall array resistance standards necessitates rigorous validation that internal quantization has not broken down without relying on the verification of dissipationless edge state transport. One proposed solution is to use a Symmetric Precision Quantization Reliability criterion, a mathematical framework that statistically assures such validation strictly through outer terminal measurements of Cn-symmetric designs. This criterion essentially bounds the likelihood of hidden localized defects arising from quantum Hall breakdown and has potential uses in quantum computing and semiconductor testing but is presented in the context of its application toward quantum electrical standards.
label: arXiv:2611.26016v1

summary.one_liner: The scaling of multi-element quantized Hall array resistance standards necessitates rigorous validation that internal quantization has not broken down without relying on the verification of dissipationless edge state transport.

title: Topology-Enabled Self-Verification of Quantum Hall Resistance Standards

abstract: Pulsar-timing accelerations point to a localized mass concentration near the Sun, consistent with a dark matter sub-halo. We work out what such an object implies for the nature of dark matter, organizing the implications by their observable effect: suppression or enhancement of structure formation, internal structure and survival after formation, and emission or scattering by the constituents. We discuss ultralight wave dark matter, thermal and nonthermal warm dark matter, dark acoustic oscillations and dark matter-baryon scattering, elastic and inelastic self-interactions, invisible decays with recoil, primordial black holes, indirect detection, and a possible connection to the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy recoil candidate. We then ask what new data would discriminate among these models. The existing accelerations are measured outside the tidal radius, where they are blind to the interior mass distribution, to the object's velocity, and to the sub-halo population. We identify four routes that lift these degeneracies: accelerations measured inside the halo, which separate point-mass, cuspy, and cored profiles; lensing and accretion, which test whether the mass is compact; the morphology of annihilation or decay emission, which probes the inner profile; and a search for a comoving stellar population, which tests whether the object is dark and measures its velocity. We also contrast this program with pulsar-timing-array searches for transiting dark matter substructure, which probe vastly lighter objects through a different observable.
label: arXiv:2611.25359v1

summary.one_liner: Pulsar-timing accelerations point to a localized mass concentration near the Sun, consistent with a dark matter sub-halo.

title: Dark Matter Model Implications of a Candidate Sub-halo Near the Sun, and the Data Needed to Discriminate Among Them

abstract: To study the early-universe production of dark matter particles beyond thermal equilibrium often requires solving several coupled Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level. We present a new method to address this challenge using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) based on stochastic interactions of an ensemble of particles. We implement and validate efficient algorithms to describe freeze-out, decays, elastic scattering and number-changing processes within the dark sector. These algorithms do not require a discretisation of momentum space on a pre-defined grid and do not rely on approximations such as thermally averaged cross sections. As illustrative example, we consider a scenario with two-step dark matter production, leading to a bimodal phase-space distribution, and consider the subsequent evolution under elastic and number-changing processes. We show that DSMC is a flexible approach to explore out-of-equilibrium processes and solve Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level in order to predict the abundance of dark matter particles and their effect on structure formation.
label: arXiv:2611.25812v1

summary.background: ['Dark matter: hypothetical, weakly interacting matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies and is inferred from gravity.', 'Freeze-out: the point in cosmic history when particles stop interacting often enough to stay in equilibrium with the hot plasma, fixing their remaining abundance.', 'Boltzmann equation: a kinetic equation describing how the number of particles at each momentum changes over time due to collisions and decays.', 'Phase-space distribution: a description of how many particles occupy each combination of position and momentum.', 'Monte Carlo simulation: a method that uses random sampling of individual particles and random event choices to estimate how a system evolves.', 'Thermal averaging: a common simplification that replaces energy-dependent interaction rates with one averaged value, which the paper avoids.']
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces a Direct Simulation Monte Carlo approach that tracks an ensemble of stochastically interacting particles to solve phase-space Boltzmann equations for dark matter production, including freeze-out, decays, elastic scattering and number-changing processes, without a fixed momentum grid or thermally averaged cross sections.
summary.plain: Dark matter particles were produced in the early universe, and predicting how many remain requires tracking how their energies and momenta spread out as they interact. Standard methods use equations that are hard to solve when the particles are far from thermal equilibrium. The authors instead simulate a large collection of individual particles that collide and transform randomly, and they test this on a scenario where dark matter is made in two steps, producing a two-peaked energy distribution. The abstract presents this as a flexible, validated method; it does not report specific numerical results in the summary provided.
summary.why: Dark matter abundance and its effect on structure formation depend on details of the particle energy distribution that simplified calculations may miss, so a more general solver could matter for cosmology. The abstract does not show how large the practical gain is over existing codes, so its significance is best judged from the full paper.

title: Direct simulation Monte Carlo for dark matter production and phase-space evolution

abstract: Massive neutron stars (NSs) require a sufficiently stiff core equation of state (EOS), while the relatively small tidal deformability inferred from GW170817 favors softer nuclear matter at intermediate densities. Given the importance of the nuclear symmetry energy in neutron-rich matter, an intriguing question arises: Can the symmetry energy become supersoft at high densities while remaining compatible with these seemingly competing constraints? Within the nonlinear Walecka framework, we demonstrate that nucleon short-range correlations (SRCs), manifested as a high-momentum tail (HMT) in the nucleon momentum distribution, can accommodate such behavior without introducing additional interaction parameters. We derive for the first time analytical expressions for the symmetry energy curvature $K_{\rm{sym}}$ for both free Fermi gas (FFG) and HMT momentum distributions. Using model parameter sets that reproduce empirical nuclear matter properties around saturation density, we find that SRC-HMT yields substantially more negative $K_{\rm{sym}}$ than the FFG case, allowing the symmetry energy to reach a maximum at low supra-saturation densities and subsequently decrease while the total pressure remains sufficient to support massive NSs. The resulting EOSs also predict smaller NS radii and tidal deformabilities consistent with GW170817. These results connect the microscopic nucleon momentum distribution with the density dependence of the symmetry energy and macroscopic NS properties.
label: arXiv:2611.25913v1

summary.one_liner: Massive neutron stars (NSs) require a sufficiently stiff core equation of state (EOS), while the relatively small tidal deformability inferred from GW170817 favors softer nuclear matter at intermediate densities.

title: Nucleon Short-Range Correlations and Supersoft Nuclear Symmetry Energy: Compatibility with Massive Neutron Stars and GW170817

abstract: u3lib is a C++ library for U(3)/SU(3) representation-theory calculations in nuclear structure and related applications. It evaluates Wigner coupling and Racah recoupling coefficients using the procedure proposed in 2024 by Dang et al., which avoids the binomial coefficients and alternating sums used in earlier formulations. The library also provides irreducible representations (irreps), dimensions, Casimir invariants, conjugation, and tensor-product decompositions with outer multiplicities. It supports the canonical Gelfand-Tsetlin basis and the physical SU(3) $\supset$ SO(3) basis, including inner multiplicities and the transformation between the two bases. Generator routines return matrix elements in the canonical basis and reduced matrix elements in the physical basis. Python bindings mirror the C++ API. Domain skills supplied with the repository allow an AI assistant with code-execution access to call these routines from natural-language requests.
label: arXiv:2611.26558v1

summary.one_liner: u3lib is a C++ library for U(3)/SU(3) representation-theory calculations in nuclear structure and related applications.

title: u3lib: An AI-Ready Computational Framework for U(3) Symmetry Algebra, Wigner Coupling, and Racah Recoupling Coefficients

abstract: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.
label: arXiv:2611.26506v1

summary.one_liner: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance.

title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding

abstract: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms. First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks. These protocols attain the optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit platforms, improving existing devices by changing only their pulse sequences. We then introduce quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which couples quantum sensors to a quantum processor. QCS combines two new primitives: a quantum computational frequency comb that coherently converts any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and a family of quantum algorithms that use the oracle to extract signal information in superposition. Variations can be implemented on current platforms with only one memory ancilla. We show that the ultimate limit imposed by quantum mechanics lies polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit, and that QCS achieves it. Attaining this new limit requires quantum computation, establishing a fundamental separation between conventional and quantum computational sensing. Moreover, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals under constant-strength sensor depolarization, while we prove that the same noise limits any protocol lacking quantum computation to standard-quantum-limit scaling. Our result provides the first asymptotic, beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology when noise is aligned with the signal, proving that Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing. Our work builds an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and establishes quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with quantum advantages that surpass the Heisenberg limit and that persist under noise.
label: arXiv:2611.25572v1

summary.one_liner: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing

abstract: We calculate numerically energy spectra and angular distributions of photoelectrons and X-ray photons emitted in the process of tunnel photoionization of argon by a focused laser beam of multi-petawatt power. By scanning the beam power and varying the degree of focusing and the field polarization, we show these distributions to be sensitive both to the peak laser intensity and to the field configuration in the focal spot. Investigated parameters of the laser beam correspond to those of several recently commissioned lasers of multi-petawatt power. These findings, in line with the earlier reported proposals, provide a basis for the development of a reliable ionization diagnostics of extremely intense laser fields.
label: arXiv:2611.26496v1
