summary.background: ["Tunnel ionization: in a very strong laser field, the electric field bends the atom's binding barrier enough that an electron can leak out of the atom.", 'Petawatt: a power of 10^15 watts, delivered in very short pulses; focusing concentrates it to extreme intensities.', 'Photoelectrons: electrons ejected from atoms by light; their energy and direction carry information about the field.', 'High-energy photons: X-rays emitted during the strong-field process, which also depend on the field.', 'Focal spot and polarization: the intensity varies across the focused beam, and the direction the electric field oscillates (polarization) changes the outcome.', "Diagnostic: a measurement used to infer a hidden physical quantity, here the laser's peak intensity and field shape."]
summary.one_liner: The authors numerically compute energy spectra and angular distributions of photoelectrons and X-ray photons from tunnel ionization of argon in focused multi-petawatt laser fields, and argue these observables track peak intensity and focal-spot field configuration as a diagnostic.
summary.plain: Very powerful lasers now produce light intensities so high that they tear electrons off atoms, and it is hard to measure exactly how intense the focused beam really is. This paper uses computer simulations of argon atoms hit by such beams to predict what the ejected electrons and emitted X-rays look like. The authors report that these electron and X-ray patterns change with the laser power, how tightly the beam is focused, and its polarization, which suggests they could be used to check the beam's properties.
summary.why: Knowing the true intensity inside the focal spot is needed to interpret experiments with the newest multi-petawatt lasers, so a reliable in-situ diagnostic would be useful. The abstract supports only a proposal with numerical predictions; whether it works in practice depends on experimental tests that the abstract does not describe.

title: Fast electrons and high energy photons produced in strong-field ionization of atoms as diagnostics of multi-petawatt laser beams

abstract: Laser-plasma accelerators reach gradients a thousand times above radio-frequency cavities, but need joule-class femtosecond lasers firing about once per second, and electrons outrun the wave. A comb of laser lines spaced by the plasma frequency, each in its own mode of a matched channel, drives a wake moving at the speed of light. In particle-in-cell simulations a 175\,mJ, 0.5\,ps drive holds 21\,GV/m over 10\,mm with a 0.15\,rad phase drift; a test electron gains 208\,MeV, 2.6 times more than in one mode. Because the wave builds up resonantly, the required energy falls steeply with density: a 29\,mJ drive sustains 20\,GV/m, and a 10\,mJ drive, within reach of kilohertz industrial lasers, gives a test electron 170\,MeV over 30\,mm. A simulated stage transfers 5\,\% of the laser energy to the wake; the Manley--Rowe limit is about 18\,\% for five lines.
label: arXiv:2611.26032v1

summary.one_liner: Laser-plasma accelerators reach gradients a thousand times above radio-frequency cavities, but need joule-class femtosecond lasers firing about once per second, and electrons outrun the wave.

title: Dephasing-free plasma acceleration with millijoule picosecond lasers

abstract: Ice-cloud retrievals from polarimetric radar, lidar and submillimeter radiometry commonly assume random orientation, horizontal alignment or a prescribed flutter angle. We link the orientation dynamics of ice crystals to their scattering. Fluid-inertial torque turns small settling crystals broadside on, and turbulent velocity gradients turn them away, so their orientation depends on the dissipation rate. We combine a closed-form orientation distribution for overdamped spheroids, including rotational diffusion and turbulence intermittency, with orientation-averaged Rayleigh, Rayleigh--Gans, T-matrix and specular scattering. Turbulence enters the scattering only through the Legendre moments of the orientation distribution. In the Rayleigh regime the specific differential phase follows crystal alignment, so assuming perfectly horizontal crystals biases ice-water-content retrievals low. Combining the specific differential phase with differential reflectivity limits this bias to $25\%$ for a single size of the shapes studied. For size distributions that span the alignment transition the bound can fail, because the two observables weight sizes differently. Depolarization adds sensitivity to higher-order moments and to intermittency. At finite size the second orientation moment mainly controls the scattering cross sections and the asymmetry parameter, and for optically soft crystals its contribution vanishes $54.7^\circ$ from the vertical. Specular returns from partly aligned plates should persist for lidars pointed $3^\circ$ from nadir. An exploratory analysis of EarthCARE lidar data finds a weakly depolarizing, low-lidar-ratio signature most frequent near $-11^\circ$C, where plates grow. Degree-scale tilt widths inferred from glints and lidar require larger crystals, near or beyond the validity range of the model.
label: arXiv:2611.25750v1

summary.one_liner: Ice-cloud retrievals from polarimetric radar, lidar and submillimeter radiometry commonly assume random orientation, horizontal alignment or a prescribed flutter angle.

title: Scattering by Small Ice Crystals in Turbulence: From Orientation Statistics to Retrieval Biases

abstract: We present a systematic study of energy transfers in three-dimensional (3D) decaying Hall-magnetohydrodynamics (HMHD) turbulence. Our study has been designed to investigate the dependence of these transfers on initial energy spectra, the ion-inertial length $d_{i}$, and the magnetic Prandtl number $Pr_{m}$. Using shell-to-shell decomposition, we compute the energy transfer rates for (a) kinetic-to-kinetic, (b) magnetic-to-magnetic, (c) kinetic-to-magnetic, and (d) magnetic-to-kinetic interactions by carrying out extensive pseudospectral direct numerical simulations (DNSs) of 3D HMHD and its MHD counterpart. Furthermore, we examine the magnetic-to-magnetic and current-density-to-magnetic energy transfers arising from the Hall term in this framework. Energy transfers between like fields -- namely, kinetic-to-kinetic and magnetic-to-magnetic -- are predominantly local and forward in direction, cascading energy from large to small length scales. This behavior is consistent with a self-similar flow structure in the inertial range. Cross-field transfers, between kinetic and magnetic energy, are found to be forward but non-local in character. At low and high $Pr_{m}$, the transfers become local, and the nonlinear energy transfer is significantly suppressed. Moreover, we observe that the Hall term drives both inverse and forward transfers of magnetic energy, associated with local and non-local transfer, respectively.
label: arXiv:2611.25686v1

summary.background: ['Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD): a fluid model treating a conducting fluid or plasma as coupled to magnetic fields.', 'Hall term: an extra term in plasma models that becomes important at scales near the ion-inertial length, where ions and electrons no longer move together.', 'Ion-inertial length d_i: the characteristic scale below which the Hall effect matters.', 'Magnetic Prandtl number Pr_m: the ratio of fluid viscosity to magnetic diffusivity, controlling how the velocity and magnetic fields dissipate relative to each other.', 'Energy cascade: energy moving from large to small length scales (forward) or the reverse (inverse), in turbulence.', 'Shell-to-shell energy transfer: a method of splitting the wavenumber spectrum into shells and measuring how much energy moves between them.', 'Pseudospectral direct numerical simulation (DNS): solving the governing equations directly on a grid with spectral accuracy, without a turbulence model.']
summary.one_liner: The paper uses pseudospectral direct numerical simulations of decaying 3D Hall-MHD turbulence, with shell-to-shell energy-transfer analysis, to show how kinetic and magnetic energy exchange depends on the ion-inertial length and the magnetic Prandtl number, and how the Hall term drives inverse and forward magnetic energy transfer.
summary.plain: Turbulence is the chaotic swirling seen in stirred liquids and in plasmas such as the solar wind, and it moves energy from big motions to small ones. This paper studies a version of turbulence in electrically conducting plasma where the 'Hall effect' (a term that matters when ions and electrons decouple at small scales) is included. Using large computer simulations, the authors track how energy flows between moving-fluid energy and magnetic energy, and how this depends on two plasma parameters.
summary.why: Energy transfer across scales is central to how plasmas heat and organize themselves, including in space and astrophysical settings, so knowing which way energy flows and whether it is local or non-local is useful. The abstract does not compare these results with observations, so any link to specific space or lab plasmas is something the authors would need to establish.

title: Energy transfers in decaying three-dimensional Hall-magnetohydrodynamics turbulence: Dependence on the Ion-Inertial Length and the Magnetic Prandtl Number

abstract: Quantitative measurement of complex coloration patterns is essential for many biological studies and practical applications. Although color perception depends on the observer's visual system, an objective characterization is possible by measuring the spectral reflectance across the sample surface. Traditional methods for measuring spectral reflectance are either limited in spatial resolution, as with spectrometer probes, or limited in spectral detail, as with digital cameras. We present a method for reconstructing spatially resolved spectral reflectance of samples from multiple images taken under different illuminants with known spectral irradiance. Using an optimization scheme that minimizes pixel-value error while regularizing for the smoothness of the reflectance spectrum, our method generates high-resolution hyperspectral images. We tested our method using both existing spectral reflectance datasets and original multi-illumination images taken in a custom photo-box, demonstrating high accuracy and simple implementation of the method, as well as the ability to infer how samples are perceived by different visual systems. Our method can be a useful tool for objective quantification of complex visual patterns in color-related biological research and imaging applications.
label: arXiv:2611.25520v1

summary.background: ['Spectral reflectance: the fraction of light a surface reflects at each wavelength, which defines its color independent of who is looking.', 'Hyperspectral imaging: capturing a full spectrum at every pixel of an image, rather than a few color channels.', 'RGB cameras: standard cameras record only three broad bands (red, green, blue), which loses much spectral detail.', 'Illuminant spectral irradiance: the known distribution of light power across wavelengths emitted by each light source; knowing it is needed to convert camera readings back to reflectance.', 'Regularization: adding a penalty, here for non-smooth spectra, so that an underdetermined inverse problem has a sensible solution.', 'Visual systems: different animals have different photoreceptors, so the same reflectance can look different to them; the method is meant to model this.']
summary.one_liner: The authors reconstruct spatially resolved spectral reflectance of samples from several ordinary photographs taken under known different illuminants, using an optimization that fits pixel values while penalizing rough reflectance spectra.
summary.plain: Color patterns on animals and objects carry information, but a normal camera records only three broad color channels, while a spectrometer measures full spectra at only one spot at a time. The authors photograph the same sample under several known light sources and computationally combine the images into a map of how much light each point reflects at each wavelength. The abstract reports high accuracy and that the method can predict how different visual systems would see the sample, though it gives no specific figures in the summary provided.
summary.why: Objective measurement of color patterns matters for studies of animal signaling, camouflage, and imaging applications, and a cheap camera-based route to full spectral maps could make such work easier. The abstract does not give quantitative accuracy results or comparisons, so the strength of the claim can't be judged from it alone.

title: Multi-Illumination Spectral Reflectance Reconstruction: A method for hyperspectral imaging using digital photography

abstract: This work investigates deep convective self-aggregation in the space of scales, extending the physical-space analysis of Part I. We introduce a novel theoretical framework by examining and deriving a generalized Yaglom equation for the second-order structure function $\langle δh_f^{\prime 2} \rangle$, the scale-dependent variance of Frozen Moist Static Energy (FMSE). Self-aggregation is found to be sustained by an inverse energy cascade driven by boundary-layer production and mediated by mesoscale circulations with horizontal scales $r \sim$(100-250 km). The inverse cascade of energy is found to be realized through a series of shallow and mid-level mesoscale circulations which behave in a self-similar way. Accordingly, the scale-energy variance exhibits an extraordinary collapse across all atmospheric layers onto a robust self-similar power law, $\langle δh_f^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{6/5}$. In contrast, horizontal velocity increments show a degree of self-similarity ($\langle δu_r^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{2/5}$) that retains a residual height dependence. Interestingly, the FMSE scaling breaks down at elevations lower than 750 m and at small local scales below 100 km, allowing us to identify the boundary layer top as a scale-dependent dividing layer where the strong stratification filters the interactions between the surface and free-troposphere, so that small scale dynamics of the low and high atmospheric layers are decoupled while those at large mesoscale are coupled. The derived scaling laws are also used to quantify the moisture-convection feedback via scale-dependent correlation coefficients that show that vertical transport strengthens with scale ($ρ_{mc\perp} \sim r^{2/5}$), while horizontal convergence weakens at the exact inverse rate ($ρ_{mc\parallel} \sim r^{-2/5}$).
label: arXiv:2611.25829v1

summary.one_liner: This work investigates deep convective self-aggregation in the space of scales, extending the physical-space analysis of Part I.

title: Multi-scale dynamics of deep convective self-aggregation. Part II: scale-by-scale budget and mesoscale self-similarity

abstract: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods, or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only. Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused, frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.
label: arXiv:2611.26095v1

summary.one_liner: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories.

title: Approximate Adjoint Models for Memory and Compute-Efficient Online Learning of Hybrid Models

abstract: We show that the traditional approach of parameterizing the background and linear-perturbation evolutions, through the equation-of-state parameter $w(a)$ and a time-dependent sound speed squared $\bar{c}^2_s(a)$, does not fully specify the cosmological behavior of dark energy theories. Using a new, fully nonlinear fluid framework, we perform spherical-collapse simulations of two clustering dark energy models with identical $w(a)$ and $\bar{c}^2_s(a)$, finding that their central dark-energy densities differ by up to 50\% for cluster-sized dark matter halos. We identify the departure of the local sound speed from $\bar{c}_s$ as the main driver of these differences. In contrast, all other theory-specific quantities in the fluid equations can be described by their background values to a very good approximation. The results demonstrate that nonlinear structure formation encodes critical additional information about the underlying dark energy theory, opening an avenue for discriminating between models using observables on small scales.
label: arXiv:2611.26460v1

summary.one_liner: We show that the traditional approach of parameterizing the background and linear-perturbation evolutions, through the equation-of-state parameter $w(a)$ and a time-dependent sound speed squared $\bar{c}^2_s(a)$, does not fully specify the cosmological behavior of dark energy theories.

title: Breaking the background and linear degeneracies: Using nonlinear clustering to discriminate between dark energy models

abstract: While the background evolution of dark energy is relatively straightforward to model, its perturbations, especially on nonlinear scales, generally require significantly more sophisticated treatment. Existing simulation methods for clustering dark energy --- a large class of interesting theories which are until now not well studied --- usually rely on grid-based solvers and perturbatively derived equations, whose validity in the nonlinear regime remains unknown. In this paper, we introduce a novel fluid method based on splitting the dark energy action into two parts: a kinetic part and a potential part. The resulting fluid equations are fully nonlinear and not reliant on simplifying approximations, making them suitable to describe the small-scale evolution of clustering dark energy theories, such as $k$-essence models with small sound speeds. We demonstrate the numerical implementation of this framework through spherical-collapse simulations of two representative $k$-essence models, evolving dark matter and dark energy simultaneously. The simulations are able to follow the development of dark-energy density perturbations throughout halo collapse, to $\mathcal{O}(\textrm{1}-10)$. By investigating their dependence on the dark-energy sound speed and dark-matter halo mass, we illustrate how dark-energy clustering responds to variations in the competing effects of pressure support and gravitational pull. These results demonstrate the applicability of this new framework to study nonlinear dark-energy clustering across a range of physical conditions, providing the foundation for its future extension to fully three-dimensional cosmological simulations through particle-based algorithms such as smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPH).
label: arXiv:2611.26461v1

summary.background: ['Dark energy: the unknown component driving the accelerating expansion of the universe; its equation of state describes its pressure relative to its energy density.', "Perturbations and clustering: small density variations that can grow under gravity into bound structures such as halos; 'nonlinear' means the growth has become large enough that simple linear approximations fail.", 'k-essence: a class of dark-energy models whose behaviour is governed by a scalar field with a non-standard kinetic term; the sound speed controls how quickly pressure fluctuations spread, and small sound speeds let the dark energy clump.', 'Action and fluid equations: the action is a single function from which field equations are derived; a fluid description treats the matter as a continuous medium with density, velocity and pressure rather than tracking the field directly.', 'Spherical collapse: an idealised model in which a uniform spherical overdensity collapses, used to test how structures form and how their density evolves.', 'Grid-based versus particle methods: grid solvers compute fields on fixed cells, while SPH represents the fluid by moving particles with smoothing kernels.']
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces a fully nonlinear fluid description of clustering dark energy, obtained by splitting the dark-energy action into kinetic and potential parts, and uses spherical-collapse simulations of two k-essence models to study how dark-energy density perturbations grow during halo collapse as the sound speed and halo mass vary.
summary.plain: Dark energy is thought to drive the accelerating expansion of the universe, and some versions of it might also clump under gravity like matter, but these clumps are hard to simulate once they become dense. The authors propose a new way to write the equations for dark energy as a fluid, built by separating its underlying action into a motion part and an energy part, so that the equations do not rely on approximations that are only valid at large scales. They test this on simple spherical collapses of two example dark-energy models, following dark matter and dark energy together, and check how the clumping depends on the dark energy's sound speed and the halo's mass.
summary.why: Most current tools for clustering dark energy rely on approximations whose validity in the dense, nonlinear regime is unknown, so a method that avoids them could matter for testing these theories against future survey data. The abstract frames the work as a foundation for later full three-dimensional simulations using particle methods such as smoothed particle hydrodynamics, but it does not show that such extension has been done.

title: Splitting the action: A fully nonlinear fluid method for clustering dark energy

abstract: We investigate the cosmic infrared background (CIB) that is expected to arise from the Population (Pop) III.1 supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation scenario, which involves early SMBH seeding via supermassive primordial star formation enabled by dark matter annihilation heating. We model the emission from Pop III.1 supermassive stars, including their growth phase, flash ionization phase, and early black hole accretion phase, as well as accompanying emission from lower-mass Pop III.2 stars. The CIB is composed of stellar and SMBH accretion disk continuum radiation, nebular continuum emission, and Ly$α$ radiation redistributed through scattering in the neutral intergalactic medium. Based on the feedback regulated Pop III.1 model of Petkova et al. (2026), our fiducial model assumes $\sim 10^5\,M_\odot$ Pop III.1 stars forming by $z_{\rm flash}=20$ with a comoving number density of $\sim0.2\,{\rm cMpc}^{-3}$. For this model, the combined stellar contribution is less than $1\%$ of existing direct and diffuse CIB measurements. However, the contribution to the CIB from $z\sim6-20$ SMBH accretion is expected to be larger than the Pop III.1 stellar component for average Eddington ratios $λ_{\text{Edd}} \sim 0.01$. Latest CIB observations place constraints of $λ_{\text{Edd}} \lesssim 0.3$ for the fiducial Pop III.1 model during these epochs.
label: arXiv:2611.25355v1

summary.one_liner: We investigate the cosmic infrared background (CIB) that is expected to arise from the Population (Pop) III.1 supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation scenario, which involves early SMBH seeding via supermassive primordial star formation enabled by dark matter annihilation heating.

title: The Cosmic Infrared Background from Population III.1 Supermassive Stars and Black Holes

abstract: Mapping the distribution of elements in the Milky Way and understanding how that distribution has changed over time can give us insight into the formation and evolution of our Galaxy. Here we use homogeneously estimated atmospheric parameters, elemental abundances, distances, and ages for ~580,000 giants from five major spectroscopic surveys---all simultaneously placed on a single, self-consistent scale by one model---allowing us, for the first time, to use a large sample of stars with uniform labels and ages that cumulatively span much of the disk to trace how the metallicity structure of the Milky Way depends on stellar age. Our chrono-chemical analysis shows that the radial metallicity gradient of the disk depends non-monotonically on age: it is shallow for the youngest stars, steepening to a maximum of ~-0.07 dex/kpc at intermediate ages (~5-6 Gyr), and flattening to near zero for the oldest stars. This "U-shaped" age dependence is driven largely by the low-alpha (thin-disk) population, with the high-alpha (thick-disk) sequence having weak gradients at all ages. In contrast to [Fe/H], the radial [Mg/Fe] gradient is weak (<~0.01 dex/kpc) at all ages. Together, these trends are consistent with an inside-out formation scenario in which the gradient of the star-forming gas has flattened over at least the last ~6 Gyr, while the near-zero gradient of the oldest stars reflects their formation in a well-mixed disk, efficient radial migration, or both.
label: arXiv:2611.26550v1

summary.one_liner: Mapping the distribution of elements in the Milky Way and understanding how that distribution has changed over time can give us insight into the formation and evolution of our Galaxy.

title: Chemical Cartography Across Time: The Age-Dependent Chemical Structure of the Milky Way with a Homogeneous Sample of 580,000 Giants from Five Surveys

abstract: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field. The dust size distribution is evolved taking into ac- count coagulation and fragmentation. For the magnetic field evolution, we considered both ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation. The MRI-driven turbulent viscosity was estimated self-consistently from the local magnetic field strength and non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics diffusivities. We found that MRI-driven turbulence becomes stronger for smaller initial plasma beta, and the enhanced tur- bulence promotes dust growth in MRI-active regions. However, dust growth is ultimately limited by radial drift, and the dependence of dust size on the magnetic field strength is significant only in the outer regions of the disk. In other words, over most of the disk, radial drift remains the dominant factor controlling the maximum dust size, and the magnetic field strength plays only a minor role in determining the overall dust size distribution.
label: arXiv:2611.25602v1

summary.one_liner: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks.

title: Dependence of Dust Growth on Magnetic field Strength in Protoplanetary Disks

abstract: Understanding the chemical diversity of exoplanet atmospheres is crucial for linking atmospheric composition to planetary formation history. Atmospheric C/O can provide clues about where and how planets form, particularly through the accretion of gas and solids across disk snowlines. Since planetary migration can change orbital distances and hence equilibrium temperatures ($T_{eq}$), investigating C/O across different planetary populations may provide insights into their formation and evolution. As observational precision improves with the JWST, the limits of standard atmospheric retrieval methods that assume altitude-independent molecular abundances have become apparent. We present atmospheric retrievals for 20 transiting planets with published JWST transmission spectra, including complementary HST spectra for targets where such data are available, spanning gas giants, warm Neptunes, and temperate/warm sub-Neptunes, to test how population-level chemical inferences depend on retrieval assumptions. Free-chemistry retrievals show a visually non-monotonic C/O-$T_{eq}$ distribution, but this apparent pattern is not statistically robust and is sensitive to sample composition. When molecular abundances are constrained by a grid of disequilibrium models, the inferred C/O distribution becomes more restricted, showing that demographic chemical trends can depend strongly on the adopted retrieval parameterization. Several hot Jupiters converge to low C/O ($\leq$ 0.05), whereas colder, cloudy planets retain broad posteriors that reflect limited information content of their spectra. Our results suggest that population-level chemical trends inferred from free-chemistry retrievals should be interpreted with caution unless sample selection, residual structure, prior sensitivity, and chemical assumptions are explicitly tested.
label: arXiv:2611.26548v1

summary.one_liner: Understanding the chemical diversity of exoplanet atmospheres is crucial for linking atmospheric composition to planetary formation history.

title: Demographic inference in exoplanet chemistry is shaped by retrieval assumptions

abstract: We investigate how the effective nucleon mass and symmetry energy affect pasta phase properties and the unified equation of state (EOS) of neutron stars. The nonuniform pasta structure is described within the self-consistent Thomas-Fermi approximation, while nucleonic interactions are treated in the relativistic mean-field framework with several typical parameter sets adopted. Our results indicate that the symmetry energy and its slope are crucial in determining the onset of pasta phases and their geometric configurations. In the high-density region where matter becomes uniform, the effective nucleon mass plays a dominant role. A larger effective nucleon mass tends to soften the EOS, which yields a smaller radius for a canonical $1.4 M_{\odot}$ neutron star and reduces the corresponding tidal deformability.
label: arXiv:2611.25666v1

summary.one_liner: We investigate how the effective nucleon mass and symmetry energy affect pasta phase properties and the unified equation of state (EOS) of neutron stars.

title: Impact of Effective Nucleon Mass and Symmetry Energy on Nuclear Pasta Phases and the Unified Equation of State of Neutron Stars

abstract: We study tidal disruptions of rotating solar-type stars by a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole with general-relativistic smoothed-particle hydrodynamics. To capture strong-field effects, we place the pericentre at a few gravitational radii of a black hole, and compare with weak-field encounters at a larger pericentre around a lighter black hole. We vary the black hole spin, the orbital inclination and the stellar rotation, using rigidly and differentially rotating stars with spin aligned, anti-aligned or perpendicular to the orbital angular momentum. In the strong field, the black hole spin decides whether a core survives on equatorial and inclined orbits, and stellar rotation reduces the surviving core in every partial disruption. At the larger pericentre, as in Newtonian studies, anti-aligned rotation instead protects the star from disruption. In both cases the tide reverses an anti-aligned spin just before pericentre. The outcome differs because in the strong field the tide keeps acting on the reversed core long after pericentre. Deep encounters leave cores spinning above break-up, which shed mass and angular momentum as they settle. Full disruptions approach the canonical fallback law, whereas the late-time slope of partial disruptions is not universal and is set by the debris energy distribution near the surviving core.
label: arXiv:2611.26043v1

summary.one_liner: We study tidal disruptions of rotating solar-type stars by a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole with general-relativistic smoothed-particle hydrodynamics.

title: Strong Field Tidal Disruptions of Rotating Stars by Spinning Black Holes

abstract: As single-aged populations containing stars spanning a range of masses but otherwise with similar properties, star clusters provide valuable testbeds for stellar evolution theory. The old, metal-rich, open cluster NGC 6791 is well studied, but the availability of asteroseismic observations of individual cluster members allows for a more in-depth analysis. Driven by mounting evidence that the solar assumption for convection used in almost all 1D stellar models is not adequate, and in light of the increased precision provided by modern data and asteroseismic constraints, we built and compared custom isochrones with varying values of the convective mixing length, $α_\text{MLT}$, to two clusters with well-determined ages: NGC 6791 and the well-studied, metal-poor globular cluster M92. For both clusters, we found that the best-fitting mixing length parameter decreases monotonically as a function of evolutionary phase, finding values between $0.98-1.10α_{\odot}$ for NGC 6791 and $1.16-1.21α_{\odot}$ for M92. In NGC 6791, this corresponds to an 18% decrease in the best fitting mixing length between the main sequence turn-off and upper end of the red giant branch. The degree of variation found within this one object is therefore comparable to variation across the literature in $α_\text{MLT}$ fits for other non-solar targets, calling single-valued $α_\text{MLT}$ fits to clusters into question. It is also consistent with $\log g$-$α_\text{MLT}$ trends predicted by higher-fidelity, 3D convection analyses. Our results therefore illustrate the need for more flexibility in our treatment of the mixing length in isochrones to properly model clusters.
label: arXiv:2611.25306v1

summary.one_liner: As single-aged populations containing stars spanning a range of masses but otherwise with similar properties, star clusters provide valuable testbeds for stellar evolution theory.

title: Sherlock 'Chrones: The Curious Case of NGC 6791 and Asteroseismic Targets Therein Reveals Mixing Length Dependence on Evolutionary Stage

abstract: Mass transfer is a highly dynamical 3D process that spans evolutionary timescales in binary stars. It is key to the production of gravitational waves through formation of binary black holes and other double compact objects. We integrate global 3D hydrodynamics into stellar evolutionary modeling to resolve mass transfer across nuclear timescales. We employ the shellular approximation in the stellar evolution code MESA to map a 3D spatial structure by equipotential shells in the Roche geometry to maintain hydrostatic equilibrium across tidally-distorted surfaces. We employ the method of time-incremented multiscale evolution to alternate between stellar evolution and 3D hydrodynamics to span large timescales with dynamical feedback. We employ this framework to examine a likely merging binary black hole progenitor system of a low-metallicity 30Msol donor star and 9.3Msol black hole from the end of the main sequence to core Carbon depletion. We modeled two complete mass transfer phases in 3D while self-consistently accounting for stellar evolution. These comprised a thermal-timescale early Case B phase and a nuclear-timescale late Case B phase. The prescription of Kolb & Ritter (1990) closely predicted the results of 3D evolution, except at the end of the first phase of mass transfer; our 3D model remained well-contained by the outer Lagrange point, despite 1D predictions of substantial L3 overflow during this stage. We find incorporating 3D hydrodynamics during Case B mass transfer did not significantly impact expected merger times. Our model never overflowed L3 as predicted by 1D prescriptions. L2/L3 outflows formed even while underflowing those equipotentials. Our model suggests these outflows can be neglected for the evolution of similar systems, but were dense enough to potentially impact X-ray observations.
label: arXiv:2611.25310v1

summary.one_liner: Mass transfer is a highly dynamical 3D process that spans evolutionary timescales in binary stars.

title: 3D Binary Evolution of a Merging Binary Black Hole Progenitor

abstract: Molecular conformation plays a central role in determining molecular properties and dynamics. Here, we report the production and conformer-resolved spectroscopy of cold calcium 3-hydroxyphenoxide radical (CaOC$_6$H$_4$-3-OH) in a cryogenic buffer-gas cell. Internal rotation of the hydroxyl group gives rise to distinct $anti$- and $syn$-conformers. The CaO moiety acts as an optical cycling center (OCC), enabling the $\widetilde A - \widetilde X$ and $\widetilde B - \widetilde X$ transitions of both conformers to be resolved by laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy. Dispersed fluorescence measurements reveal diagonal vibrational branching fractions of 0.91-0.93, indicating favorable optical cycling characteristics. Following excitation of off-diagonal vibronic transitions near the calculated torsional barrier in the $\widetilde A$ state, the emission remains predominantly conformer specific, indicating that conformational identity is largely preserved over the excited-state fluorescence lifetime. These results demonstrate that a metal-centered OCC can serve as an intrinsic, site-specific optical reporter of molecular conformation, providing a foundation for repetitive optical readout and studies of conformational dynamics at the single-molecule level.
label: arXiv:2611.25851v1

summary.one_liner: Molecular conformation plays a central role in determining molecular properties and dynamics.

title: Witnessing Molecular Conformation via Optical Cycling Centers

abstract: We present three global adiabatic potential energy surfaces (PESs) for the O($^3$P) + C$_2$(X $^1Σ_g^+$, a $^3Π_u$) to CO(X$^1Σ^+$) + C($^3$P) reaction, computed at the icMRCI+Q/aug-cc-pVTZ level. This reaction is relevant to combustion chemistry, atmospheric processes, and astrochemistry. Since the energy difference between the $^1Σ_g^+$ and $^3Π_u$ states of C$_2$ is smaller than the zero-point energy, both states mix upon interaction with the approaching O atom. Consequently, the PESs exhibit a double-well topography in the reactant valley. Beyond this feature, the three PESs display markedly different topographies. The 1 $^3A''$ PES features a deep minimum 7.16 eV below the O + C$_2$ entrance channel. In contrast, the 2 $^3A''$ and 1 $^3A'$ surfaces possess shallower collinear wells ($\approx$ 5.7 eV) and strong angular anisotropy arising from avoided crossings with higher-lying triplet states. The analytical fits reproduce the \textit{ab initio} data with root-mean-square (RMS) deviations of 0.022--0.028 eV over an energy interval exceeding 13 eV. Quasiclassical trajectory (QCT) calculations reveal higher reactivity on the barrierless $1\,^3A''$ surface compared to the $2\,^3A''$ PES, where an angle-dependent entrance barrier reduces the cross sections. Furthermore, cross sections for reactions initiated from C$_2$(X $^1Σ_g^+$) and C$_2$(a $^3Π_u$) are remarkably similar for the three PESs, regardless of the initial rovibrational state.
label: arXiv:2611.26233v1

title: Triplet adiabatic potential energy surfaces for the O($^3$P) + C$_2$(X$^1Σ_g^+$, a$^3Π_u$) reaction and quasiclassical trajectory dynamics

abstract: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.
label: arXiv:2611.26186v1

summary.one_liner: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence.

title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery

abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.
label: arXiv:2611.25779v1

summary.one_liner: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing.

title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures

abstract: Soft biological materials are a fascinating kind of matter characterized by the unique ability of consuming internal energy to perform complex tasks to preserve the life of the single organism or a whole community. Moreover, biologically inspired materials able to mimic specific features of biological systems can be exploited to design novel materials with vast potential applications in areas ranging from healthcare and robotics to energy and environmental sustainability. In this review, we focus on the modeling approaches used to capture the dynamics of this peculiar kind of active matter, starting from the observation of orientational symmetries and reviewing the basis of the so-called active liquid crystal theory, a celebrated model that was successfully used to interpret and investigate a number of different phenomena occurring in both biological and artificial realizations. We review the role of topological defects in biological systems and discuss the complex phenomenon of active turbulence, a chaotic dynamical regime observed in a variety of different realizations of systems of both biological and synthetic origin. Finally, we discuss how geometrical and topological confinement can also play an important role in many biological processes, from cellular apoptosis in epithelial tissue, to animal morphogenesis.
label: arXiv:2611.25959v1

summary.background: ['Soft matter: materials such as gels, polymers, liquid crystals, and tissues that deform easily under small forces.', 'Active matter: systems whose constituents consume energy and generate their own motion, unlike passive materials that only respond to outside forces.', 'Liquid crystals: fluids whose elongated molecules share a preferred direction (orientation), which can be described by a continuous field.', 'Topological defects: points or lines where the orientation pattern cannot be smoothly continued, similar to a whirlpool or a hair whorl.', 'Active turbulence: chaotic, swirling flow produced by self-driven particles, distinct from the turbulence of ordinary fluids.', 'Confinement: restricting a material to a small or oddly shaped space, such as a cell or a tissue boundary, which can change its behavior.']
summary.one_liner: This review surveys modeling approaches for active matter in soft biological and bio-inspired materials, focusing on active liquid crystal theory, topological defects, active turbulence, and the effects of geometric and topological confinement.
summary.plain: Living things and some engineered materials can use stored energy to move, reshape, and organize themselves, which makes them behave differently from ordinary soft matter like rubber or gels. This review looks at the mathematical models scientists use to describe these self-driven materials, especially a framework borrowed from liquid crystals that tracks how their molecular or cellular orientations line up. It also covers chaotic, swirling flow patterns called active turbulence, the role of defects where orientation patterns break down, and how confinement in tissues and cells can influence processes such as cell death and the shaping of embryos. The abstract describes the scope of the review rather than reporting new experimental results.
summary.why: Active matter is a growing bridge between physics, biology, and materials engineering, and models that explain both living tissue and synthetic swimmers could guide the design of robots and self-organizing materials. The abstract does not show specific new findings, so its value lies mainly in consolidating the field's theoretical toolkit.

title: Soft biological and bio-inspired materials

abstract: Branched macromolecular architectures are ubiquitous in living systems and synthetic polymeric systems, create topologically complex media that strongly influence tracer dynamics beyond simple packing fraction-driven crowding effects. Motivated by biological systems such as amoebae, astrocytes, cytoskeletal assemblies, and cyclic bottlebrushes, we investigate active and passive tracer transport in polymeric environments of topologically distinct architectures. Here, using Langevin dynamics simulations, we focus on how polymer topology alters diffusion behavior in a branched-ring polymeric (BRP) environment. To isolate the role of intramolecular topology from monomer density, we specifically benchmark the BRP dynamics against an unlinked linear-ring polymer mixture (LRM). In general, we find that while passive tracers are largely unaffected by the polymer connectivity and bending rigidity, the self-propelled active tracers strongly distinguish between the two architectures. Increasing chain rigidity facilitates active diffusion in the unlinked LRM but strongly restricts mobility in the BRP matrix, driving a transition to pronounced long-time subdiffusion that becomes more prominent with propulsion strength. Different physical observables reveal that interconnected topological cages are formed in the stiff limit, leading to transient weak ergodicity breaking and leptokurtic displacement statistics. Further, the self-intermediate scattering function confirms that the short-range dynamics remain unaltered by the matrix connectivity, while relaxation at large spatial length scales is governed by the topological caging. Finally, varying the branch length and number, we identified an optimal branch architecture that maximizes active trapping. Our results establish that macromolecular connectivity and stiffness dominate the active transport even in the system of identical packing fraction.
label: arXiv:2611.25528v1

summary.background: ['Tracer: a small particle followed to measure how a medium moves things through it.', 'Active (self-propelled) tracer: a particle that drives its own motion, like a swimming cell, rather than only being pushed around by thermal jiggling.', 'Passive tracer: a particle moving only from random thermal kicks.', 'Ring polymer: a large molecule closed into a loop; branched ring polymers have loops with side arms attached.', 'Packing fraction and monomer density: how much of the space is filled by the molecules; here the two systems are matched on this so only connectivity differs.', 'Subdiffusion: motion that spreads more slowly over time than ordinary random walking.', "Weak ergodicity breaking: a state where a particle's time average no longer matches its ensemble average, meaning it stays in one region for very long periods.", 'Leptokurtic displacement statistics: step-length distributions with more very short and very long jumps than a Gaussian, a sign of heterogeneous trapping.', 'Langevin dynamics: a simulation method that models particle motion with friction and random noise.', "Self-intermediate scattering function: a measure of how a particle's position decorrelates across a given length scale over time."]
summary.one_liner: Langevin dynamics simulations compare passive and self-propelled (active) tracer diffusion in a matrix of branched ring polymers versus an unlinked mixture of linear rings at equal monomer density, finding that chain stiffness and connectivity trap active tracers and produce long-time subdiffusion and transient weak ergodicity breaking.
summary.plain: Many cells and synthetic materials are filled with tangled, branched large molecules that act like a crowded maze for anything moving through them. This paper uses computer simulations to ask how the shape and connectivity of these molecules, rather than just how crowded they are, change the movement of tiny particles, including self-propelled ones that move on their own like swimming microbes. The authors report that passive particles barely notice the difference, but self-propelled particles get stuck in cages formed by the connected branches when the chains are stiff, and an intermediate branch design traps them most effectively.
summary.why: It suggests that molecular topology alone can control how active particles get trapped, which may matter for understanding transport inside cells and for designing soft materials. The abstract is based only on simulations, so how well the findings carry over to real biological or synthetic systems is not shown here.

title: Topological trapping of active tracers in branched ring polymer matrices

abstract: Identifying active molecules for known targets and potential targets for existing drugs is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Drug-target interaction (DTI) models can rank vast numbers of drug-target pairs, but limited experimental capacity restricts testing to a small number of candidates. We compared the bidirectional recommendations of 13 released systems across 711 molecular structures of FDA-approved drugs and 614 human proteins. For the same target or drug, pairs of models produced completely disjoint Top-10 molecule and protein lists in 77.8% and 70.1% of comparisons, respectively. Even where recommendations overlapped, agreement between some systems largely reflected recurring preferences for the same candidates. Published inhibition measurements for 79 molecules and 65 kinases revealed that some systems enriched active candidates, yet their hit yields changed little when recommendations were matched to different drugs or targets, whereas other systems lost substantially more hits. Some of the former systems also rarely ranked both molecules and kinases correctly when two drugs favoured different kinases. We further retrained the same architecture on the same data, with the training objective fixed and random seeds varied. Despite similar test performance, mean pairwise Top-10 overlap on a separate screening catalogue was about two candidates. Our study moves DTI model evaluation beyond benchmark performance to assess whether model predictions can guide meaningful experimental decisions in drug discovery and target identification.
label: arXiv:2611.26369v1

summary.one_liner: Identifying active molecules for known targets and potential targets for existing drugs is central to drug discovery and repurposing.

title: From Benchmarks to the Bench: Preference, Correspondence and Selectivity in Bidirectional Drug-Target Screening

abstract: Foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials are trained on large, diverse DFT datasets, but their validation rests on equilibrium states, which does not guarantee correct emergent behavior in large-scale molecular dynamics. Where no direct experimental validation is available, comparisons to physically motivated potentials are valuable for drawing insight. We distinguish static properties, which are thermally accessible, from emergent properties, which require work from an external fatigue stress to drive rare events, and compare the potentials on both. An EAM potential and the NequIP foundational potential both agree closely with reference data for many near-equilibrium properties, but NequIP predicts an anomalously low intrinsic stacking fault energy ($\sim7$ times lower than EAM) and thus predicts far more plastic deformation under fatigue cycling of a nanoscale flaw modeled after the classical Griffith crack problem. Per-atom energy distributions after loading show that the two potentials differ most at energies far above what is thermally accessible. We also document memory-related crashes and silent extrapolation as practical concerns for practitioners of these foundational model forms.
label: arXiv:2611.26533v1

title: Emergent Fatigue Dynamics from Foundational Interatomic Potentials

abstract: A key question in the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life is the nature of the compartment that separates and protects the RNA from its environment. While membranes are a leading candidate for the initial compartment, biomolecular condensates have been proposed as an alternative, possibly simpler route to compartments. Here we show that bona fide liquid condensates form spontaneously when nucleotides (such as ATP) are mixed with divalent cations and a short-chain alcohol or diol in water. These condensates do not require any polymer to form, but can concentrate polymers like RNA and DNA, which show unexpected chemical behavior inside the condensates. Most surprisingly, RNA survives for days inside nucleotide condensates under acidic conditions that cause rapid and extensive hydrolysis in bulk. This effect is also observed for a phosphate-ester model substrate and therefore likely reflects the suppression of backbone cleavage. Coarse-grained simulations suggest that the condensate interior is bound together by magnesium-phosphate bridging interactions and is therefore highly depleted of water. At neutral pH, the same compartment reverses the course of a hammerhead ribozyme reaction, shifting it from cleavage toward religation. Finally, we observe that nucleotide droplets also spontaneously organize phospholipids at their surface, suggesting a possible evolutionary route from biomolecular condensates toward membranes. Thus, we believe that nucleotide condensates, which are built from the same building blocks as the genetic polymers themselves, overcome long-standing challenges with the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life by protecting nucleic acids and reshaping their chemistry.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767475 v1

summary.one_liner: A key question in the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life is the nature of the compartment that separates and protects the RNA from its environment.

title: Unexpected properties of nucleotide condensates could facilitate the RNA world

abstract: Controlling signaling enzymes with small molecules is a central goal in chemical biology and is of great utility for engineering cell-derived immunotherapies. Yet strategies for conferring selective small-molecule sensitivity without disrupting a protein's native function remain limited. Here we present a generalizable approach to engineering small molecule-controlled multidomain protein kinases. Using deep mutational scanning of full-length Lck, a tyrosine kinase essential for T cell receptor (TCR) signaling, we measured the effect of nearly all single amino acid substitutions in the kinase domain on phosphotransferase activity. The resulting activity landscape defined the domain's tolerance to substitution, mapped the regulatory interfaces that tune phosphotransferase activity, and, by treating bulky substitutions as ligand proxies, nominated cryptic pockets where covalent liganding is predicted to allosterically inhibit Lck. In parallel screens, we measured the sensitization of each variant to five clinically approved, reversible drugs: dabrafenib, erlotinib, gefitinib, imatinib, and nilotinib. Together, these landscapes identified substitutions that preserved or enhanced activity while sensitizing Lck to inhibition. Sensitizing substitutions were distributed throughout the kinase domain, including positions more than 30 [A] from the ATP-binding site, implicating long-range allosteric networks linking distal perturbations to ATP-binding site conformation and inhibitor potency. Integrating the activity and sensitization landscapes yielded a nilotinib-sensitized variant, I312S, that supports TCR signaling and, upon drug treatment, selectively suppresses proximal signaling and IL-2 production in Jurkat cells even in the presence of endogenous Lck.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766442 v1

summary.one_liner: Controlling signaling enzymes with small molecules is a central goal in chemical biology and is of great utility for engineering cell-derived immunotherapies.

title: Paired Deep Mutational Scanning of Lck Activity and Inhibitor Sensitivity Enables the Engineering of Pharmacological Control of T Cell Receptor Signaling

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest cancers, largely due to its poor response to chemotherapy and the development of drug resistance. Survivin (BIRC5), an inhibitor of apoptosis frequently overexpressed in PDAC, contributes to tumor cell survival and gemcitabine resistance, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for the delivery of preassembled spCas13b ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) to achieve transient and sequence-specific RNA silencing in pancreatic cancer cells. We optimized ionizable lipid formulations for Cas13b RNP encapsulation and identified a formulation achieving approximately 80% encapsulation efficiency, with sustained colloidal stability and gene-silencing activity during seven days of storage at 4{degrees}C. LNP-delivered Cas13b RNPs efficiently silenced endogenous BIRC5 in three pancreatic cancer cell lines, reducing survivin protein levels and inducing apoptosis. In gemcitabine-resistant PANC-1 cells, BIRC5 silencing synergistically enhanced the cytotoxic effect of gemcitabine in vitro. This therapeutic combination was further evaluated in a PANC-1 xenograft model, where only the combined administration of BIRC5-targeting Cas13b RNP-LNPs and gemcitabine significantly inhibited tumor growth, without apparent systemic toxicity. Intratumoral administration also restricted nanoparticle distribution to the injected tumors. These findings establish LNP-mediated delivery of Cas13b RNPs as a new strategy for transient RNA-targeted therapy and provide proof of concept for combining survivin silencing by Cas13b with chemotherapy to address gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767627 v1

title: Lipid nanoparticle-delivered Cas13b ribonucleoproteins targeting survivin overcome gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer

abstract: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767145 v1

summary.one_liner: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation.

title: DRAFT: graph-recurrent learning of dynamic gene regulatory networks along single-cell multi-omics trajectories

abstract: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types. Differentiation pathways arrange into a hierarchical, tree-like organization: regressions from specialized to undifferentiated cell types rarely occur and undifferentiated cell types often have the potential to produce, when subject to distinct stimuli, two or more differently specialized cell types. How cell type transitions acquire such a peculiar disposition requires an explanation that must reside in the properties of gene regulatory networks (GRNs); after all, GRNs orchestrate the changes in gene activity that define cell types. We studied vast numbers of small dynamic model networks to search for elementary GRNs that could yield the simplest hierarchical, developmental-like, differentiation patterns. We found that only a small minority of GRNs are compatible with hierarchical cell type transitions. Importantly, GRNs that yielded developmental-like differentiation patterns shared common traits: One is the presence of tangles of cycles of positive interactions. Genes in such a tangle produce an all-or-none one-way response to a signal. Another such trait is mutual inhibition between genes associated to different specialized cell types, enforcing their mutually exclusive activation. Moreover, these regulatory patterns are more abundant in published experimentally sustained developmental GRNs than as expected by chance. In addition, we show that it is easy to maintain hierarchical cellular differentiation throughout evolution, even when undergoing changes in gene regulatory interactions and developmental mechanisms. Our work supports the prevalence of design principles that organize hierarchically differentiation pathways in clonal multicellular organisms.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767571 v1

summary.one_liner: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types.

title: Gene regulatory networks and the organization of cell differentiation in multicellular organisms

abstract: Neuroscience relies on diverse model species to understand animal behavior and brain function. Yet, tools for rapid, high-resolution brain connectivity mapping remain unavailable in most vertebrate species, slowing progress in many neuroscience models and rendering cross-species circuit comparisons challenging. Here, we overcome this barrier by establishing sequencing-based barcoded connectomics for rapid single-neuron tracing in seven vertebrate species ranging from frogs to birds to non-human primates. We develop a general solution to viral tropism and barcode trafficking, validate our reagents by mapping the projections of thousands of neurons in the songbird HVC, and discover a single set of reagents that functions across highly divergent species. Together, we provide ready-to-use barcoding reagents for diverse species and a simple framework for further adapting them if necessary, enabling high throughput single-neuron tracing across vertebrates.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767886 v1

summary.background: ['Connectomics: mapping which neurons connect to which, often at the level of individual cells.', 'Viral tracing: a modified virus is injected into one brain area, spreads to connected neurons, and reveals their projections.', 'Barcoding: each virus particle carries a unique short DNA tag, so sequencing the tags shows which starting neurons reached which target sites, letting many neurons be traced in parallel.', 'Viral tropism: the tendency of a virus to infect certain cell types; it varies between species, which is a main obstacle to using one tool across animals.', 'Model species: animals such as mice, zebra finches or macaques that labs use because their biology is well studied.']
summary.one_liner: The authors adapt sequencing-based barcoded connectomics, which tags single neurons' long-range projections with DNA barcodes, so it works across seven vertebrate species from frogs to primates, and they report a single reagent set that functions across divergent species.
summary.plain: Neuroscientists learn how brains are wired mostly in a few well-studied animals, because detailed wiring maps are hard to make in others. This paper tries to make a fast, high-resolution wiring-mapping method work in seven vertebrate species, from frogs and birds to monkeys. The authors report a fix for a practical problem: getting the delivery viruses to infect the right cells and carry their tags properly in each species. They test this by mapping the projections of thousands of neurons in a songbird brain region, and say one set of reagents works across very different species.
summary.why: If the reagents work as described, they could let researchers compare the same kind of brain circuit across animals that are far apart on the evolutionary tree, which is hard to do today. The abstract does not give per-species results, success rates, or detailed comparisons, so how reliably the method transfers to each species cannot be judged from it alone.

title: Universal barcoded connectomics for massively parallel single-neuron projection mapping in diverse vertebrate species

abstract: Learning is commonly explained by changes in synaptic strength. In animals, however, learning also engages intrinsic plasticity -- changes in how readily neurons convert synaptic input into firing. Its contribution to human learning has been unclear, because conventional non-invasive measures of cortical excitability primarily reflect synaptic strength. Here we used controllable-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation to estimate two biophysical indices of intrinsic excitability in human motor cortex, before and after motor training. Training produced signatures of increased intrinsic excitability, selectively in the cortical representation of the trained muscle, but not an untrained muscle. Individuals showing larger intrinsic excitability changes learned faster, independently of changes in motor-evoked potential amplitude, an index of synaptic excitability that increased following training but did not predict learning rate. An axon model reproduced the measured changes through small shifts in membrane excitability. These findings provide evidence that intrinsic plasticity is expressed in the intact human brain, and that it represents a behaviourally relevant component of learning-related cortical adaptation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767269 v1

title: Motor learning engages intrinsic plasticity in the human cortex

abstract: Recent advances in single-cell and single-molecule sequencing have enabled high-resolution characterization of epigenetic states. However, methods that jointly measure multiple layers of epigenetic regulation within the same molecules and cells remain limited. Here, we developed Chromatin Immuno-Methylation sequencing (ChIMe-seq), a multimodal approach that simultaneously profiles histone modifications, DNA methylation, and nucleosome positioning genome-wide in single molecules and single cells. In contrast to recent approaches that rely on enzymatic fragmentation, ChIMe-seq preserves long DNA molecules by using a methyltransferase to deposit exogenous methylation marks that report on proximal histone modifications. This enables integration of multiple epigenetic features within individual molecules and supports short-read, long-read, and single-cell sequencing. These multimodal measurements are integrated into a novel mathematical framework that captures the coupling between nucleosome positioning, histone modifications, and DNA methylation. Both single-molecule and single-cell analyses reveal that DNA methylation is linked to nucleosome density in a manner modulated by local histone modifications, whilst differences in nucleosome:DNA structures are observed depending on epigenetic context and cell-type. Together, these results establish ChIMe-seq as a framework to investigate multifaceted epigenetic coordination across scales, from single-nucleotide resolution to long-range chromatin organization in single molecules and single cells.

abstract: Gene regulation is commonly modeled at the gene level, yet genes express multiple isoforms from distinct transcription start sites whose regulatory architecture is not resolved by current approaches. Here we introduce FULL-seq, a scalable single-cell multiomic platform that jointly profiles chromatin accessibility and full-length transcript coverage from the same cell, enabling direct coupling of regulatory elements to alternative first exon (AFE) usage. FULL-seq achieves high sensitivity for both transcriptome and chromatin accessibility while providing transcript-wide coverage across mRNAs up to 15 kb with precise exon-level mapping. We uncover diverse promoter-AFE regulatory architectures, revealing distinct transcription factor programs across alternative first exons of the same gene, and show that gene-level annotation frameworks can obscure regulatory relationships in multi-promoter genes. Applying FULL-seq to human cancer cells further reveals metastasis-associated AFE programs that are not apparent from gene-level expression. These AFE programs were reproduced in independent colorectal cancer cell-line datasets, and CALB1 AFE activation was observed in a subset of liver metastases from an independent patient cohort. Furthermore, CRISPRi-mediated repression of metastasis-associated CALB1 AFEs reduced colorectal cancer cell migration. Together, our findings establish alternative promoter and first-exon usage as a functionally relevant layer of gene regulation and demonstrate that FULL-seq enables regulatory relationships and cellular phenotypes to be connected at the promoter-isoform level.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767299 v1

abstract: We propose a semi-mechanistic ODE-based transcription model for zebrafish embryogenesis that captures common baseline expression dynamics by integrating the maternal-to-zygotic transition mechanism. We fitted this model to a time-course RNA-seq dataset of D. rerio spanning early developmental stages until 120 hpf. Using the inferred model parameters, we identified common gene expression pattern using fuzzy c-means clustering and compared these with clusters stemming from a shape-based approach using smooth trajectories. We show that the ODE-parameter-based approach improves to biological interpretability by linking clusters to underlying regulatory mechanism, such as the timing of zygotic genome activation, thereby generating more precise expression clusters. However, the results also revealed technical biases of the time-course data, originating from the poly(A) enrichment step.

abstract: The vitreous, the largest intraocular tissue, provides a transparent light path and maintains the intraocular homeostasis. The reconstitution of the vitreous in vitro or in vivo remains an unsolved biomedical challenge. Here, we discovered a common feature, the "growth edge", constituted primarily of fibroblasts and their secreted proteins in human and mouse vitreous development. By leveraging the transforming growth factor beta signaling, we then generated centimeter-scale vitreous-like organoids (VOs) through stepwise differentiation from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). The VOs exhibited striking similarity to human vitreous in terms of physical transparency, vitreoretinal interface, molecular composition, biological profiles and regenerative transplantability. Lines of evidence supported that fibroblasts are the key cell hub for vitreous development. Finally, VOs with a transthyretin (TTR) mutation recapitulated the vitreous phenotypes of human patients with vitreous amyloidosis. Together, vitreous organoid technology opens avenues for future studies of human vitreous development, disease modeling, and regenerative therapeutics for a broad spectrum of human vitreoretinal diseases.

abstract: The emergence of plasmid-mediated resistance to critically important antimicrobials poses a growing threat to global health. Here we report the first genomic evidence of plasmid-mediated fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 coexisting with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli from clinically healthy broiler chickens in Pakistan. Among 1,677 high-quality genomes collected through antimicrobial resistance surveillance in Punjab, Pakistan, three isolates recovered between 2022 and 2024 harboured all four resistance determinants. Hybrid genome assemblies showed that fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 were co-located on IncHI2A plasmids, whereas mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) were carried on separate IncI2 and IncFIA/IncFIC plasmids, all predicted to be conjugative; in one isolate the tet(X4) contig did not circularise. The isolates belonged to sequence type 93 and exhibited resistance to fosfomycin, colistin, tigecycline and cefotaxime. Comparative genomic analysis revealed highly conserved IncHI2A plasmid backbones, with an additional integron-associated resistance region in the 2024 isolates, suggesting acquisition of accessory resistance determinants. Resistance to three last-line antimicrobial classes and a canonical virulence profile now coexist on conjugative plasmids in poultry E. coli, a combination that favours co-selection and argues for plasmid-resolved surveillance in poultry production.

abstract: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) preserve native three-dimensional lung architecture and cellular complexity, providing a valuable ex vivo platform for studying pulmonary host-pathogen interactions. However, existing PCLS infection models typically introduce microorganisms into previously uninfected tissue, while fresh PCLS prepared from infected lungs have limited experimental flexibility and scalability. To our knowledge, cryopreserved PCLS generated from lungs with an established in vivo pulmonary infection have not been described. Herein, we evaluated cryopreserved PCLS from mice with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia (PCP) as an ex vivo platform for infection and therapeutic studies. PCLS were prepared from dexamethasone-immunosuppressed mice with established PCP, rested for 24 h, cryopreserved in a novel freezing medium for 12 days in liquid nitrogen, rapidly thawed, recovered for 24 h, and treated with pentamidine for 72 h. Viability was assessed in uninfected and PCP-infected PCLS before and after cryopreservation. Although post-thaw viability decreased in both groups, substantial viability was still retained, allowing further experimentation. qPCR showed that cryopreservation did not alter expression of the type I and type II alveolar epithelial markers podoplanin (Pdpn) and surfactant protein C (Sftpc) in either group. Importantly, pentamidine significantly reduced Pneumocystis mitochondrial small subunit (mtSSU) rRNA levels in thawed PCP-infected PCLS, demonstrating suitability for anti-Pneumocystis drug testing. These findings establish the first cryopreserved ex vivo PCP model using infected mouse PCLS, preserving endogenous fungal burden and infection-associated host responses while enabling flexible, scalable studies of Pneumocystis biology, host-pathogen interactions, therapeutic efficacy, and potentially other pulmonary infections.
