abstract: Metastasis requires cancer cells to overcome anchorage dependence and rewire mechanosensing pathways. Here, we identify the ERM proteins ezrin, radixin, and moesin as key but antagonistic regulators of breast cancer metastasis. Expression profiling across matched low- and high-metastatic breast cancer models revealed consistent upregulation of all three ERM proteins in highly metastatic cells. Despite this, ezrin depletion reduced colony formation, invasion, and lung metastasis, whereas radixin or moesin depletion enhanced these phenotypes. Loss of radixin or moesin increased ezrin localization at the cell edge, while ezrin depletion reduced membrane-associated moesin, indicating a dynamic balance among ERM proteins. Ezrin depletion also increased focal adhesion size and number, FAK activation, and force transmission to the extracellular matrix, whereas radixin or moesin silencing produced opposite effects. Cellular force magnitude was inversely correlated with invasion, and pharmacological modulation of contractility reverted the effects of ERM depletion. These findings reveal an ERM-dependent mechanosensing checkpoint that regulates metastasis through control of adhesion dynamics and force transmission.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767111 v1

summary.background: ['Metastasis: the spread of cancer from its original site to distant organs, such as the lungs.', 'Anchorage dependence: normal cells need to attach to a surface to grow; metastatic cells must loosen this requirement.', 'Mechanosensing: how cells detect and respond to physical forces from their environment.', 'Focal adhesions: small anchor points where a cell grips the extracellular matrix, the mesh of proteins around cells.', 'ERM proteins: ezrin, radixin and moesin, which link the cell membrane to the actin cytoskeleton (the internal scaffold of the cell).', 'FAK (focal adhesion kinase): a signalling enzyme that becomes activated at focal adhesions and helps drive cell movement.', "Contractility: the ability of the cell's internal scaffold to pull, which generates the forces transmitted outward."]
summary.one_liner: The paper reports that in breast cancer models the three ERM proteins (ezrin, radixin, moesin) rise together in highly metastatic cells yet act in opposite directions, with ezrin loss reducing and radixin or moesin loss enhancing invasion, colony formation, and lung metastasis, linked to changes in focal adhesions, FAK activation, and force transmission to the matrix.
summary.plain: Cancer spreads when cells break loose and travel to new organs, and they must sense and pull on their surroundings to do so. This study looks at three related proteins, ezrin, radixin and moesin, that help link a cell's internal skeleton to its outer membrane. The authors found that all three are more abundant in highly spreading breast cancer cells, but removing ezrin reduced spread in their tests while removing radixin or moesin increased it, with the effects tied to how strongly cells pull on their surroundings.
summary.why: It suggests that the three proteins are not simply interchangeable markers of cancer spread but can have opposing roles, which matters if anyone tries to target them therapeutically. The abstract does not say whether these findings hold in human tumours or other cancer types, so the translational reach is unclear.

title: ERM proteins antagonistically control cancer invasion and metastasis via mechanosensing regulation

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal cancers in the western world and is largely resistant to treatment. A major barrier to effective treatment is the highly desmoplastic and immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment, where the organisation of tumour, stromal and resident immune cells limit immune infiltration. B7-H3 (CD276) is an emerging immune checkpoint marker investigated in phase I and Ib/2 clinical trials in PDAC, yet its biological role within the tumour environment remains poorly understood. We performed an integrated multiscale spatial profiling study to map B7-H3 expression across regional and single-cell spatial contexts in treatment-naive resected human PDAC. Furthermore, we explored the B7-H3 landscape in the neoadjuvant setting. Our results demonstrate that B7-H3 is not simply overexpressed in cancer but may act as a spatial organiser of the PDAC microenvironment, associated with a transition from epithelial-intrinsic tumour architecture to fibro-inflammatory immune states that underpin immune suppression, aggressive disease and poor prognosis. This fibro-inflammatory state appears conserved within the neoadjuvant landscape.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.762837 v1

abstract: Variation within populations is ubiquitous in nature, yet many models and frameworks in community ecology assume that all individuals within a population interact with the community identically. Modern coexistence theory is no exception; however, several subfields of ecology have independently been integrating coexistence theory, each asking the same underlying question: how do structured population dynamics shape coexistence outcomes? Here, I propose a unifying framework for integrating population variation into modern coexistence theory that is applicable across all fields of ecology. The application of this framework is presented in three case studies: niche overlap and fitness differences between influenza substrains, mutual invasibility between competing perennial plants, and fluctuation-dependent invasion outcomes in apparently competing prey with a foraging-predation risk tradeoff. Together, these examples illustrate the framework's broad applicability, power to resolve the interaction between population and community level processes, and its potential to reveal novel ecological phenomena.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766574 v1

summary.background: ['Coexistence theory asks why different species can persist together in the same place instead of one driving the others out.', 'Modern coexistence theory often separates stabilizing mechanisms (species limit their own growth more than that of rivals) from fitness differences (some species are simply better competitors).', 'Invasion tests check whether each species can increase when rare, which is a common way to decide whether coexistence is possible.', 'Structured populations are groups whose members differ in traits such as age, size, strain, or behavior, rather than being identical.', 'Niche overlap measures how much two species rely on the same resources.', 'A foraging-predation risk tradeoff means feeding more exposes an animal to predators, so animals must balance food gain against danger.']
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a general framework for extending modern coexistence theory to account for variation among individuals within populations, and illustrates it with three case studies (influenza substrains, perennial plants, and prey with a foraging-predation risk tradeoff).
summary.plain: Ecologists often model a species as if every individual behaves the same way toward its competitors, but real populations contain varied individuals, and that variation can affect whether species can live together. The author proposes a single framework for building this within-population variation into the existing modern coexistence theory, which is meant to work across different areas of ecology. The abstract presents three example applications, but it does not report specific numerical results, so the strength of the findings cannot be judged from it alone.
summary.why: Several subfields of ecology have been working on this same question separately, so a shared framework could help them compare results and connect population-level and community-level processes. Whether it delivers on that promise depends on the detailed case studies, which the abstract only summarizes.

title: A unifying framework for structured population dynamics in modern coexistence theory

abstract: Modern coexistence theory (MCT) has been the mainstay of recent research on coexistence of competing species. Competition not only drives evolutionary changes in traits that affect coexistence, but also induces rapid plastic changes. However, a generalised framework that integrates plasticity and evolution into MCT is lacking. We formulate such a framework for a system of two competing species and analyse how breadth of available resources modulates the effect of competition-induced plasticity on the evolution of coexistence components (niche and fitness difference). We find that, in broad environments, divergent plasticity accelerates evolution towards positive invasion growth rates for both species, facilitating coexistence, whereas convergent plasticity hinders this process. Surprisingly, in narrower environments, divergent plasticity can hinder coexistence, leading to exclusion, whereas convergent plasticity can facilitate coexistence. Our results show that plasticity reshapes the eco-evolutionary trajectories to coexistence, highlighting the importance of integrating short-term plastic responses with long-term evolutionary dynamics.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767819 v1

summary.background: ['Coexistence theory: a framework asking when competing species can persist together, usually decomposed into niche difference (how much they differ in resource use) and fitness difference (how evenly matched they are).', 'Invasion growth rate: how fast a rare species grows when competing with the common one; a positive value means it can recover and so coexist.', 'Phenotypic plasticity: an individual changing its traits (such as feeding or behaviour) during its life in response to its surroundings, as opposed to genetic change over generations.', 'Evolution of coexistence components: the idea that natural selection can shift niche and fitness differences over time, so coexistence can emerge or fail through evolution.', "Divergent versus convergent plasticity: whether competition pushes the two species' traits further apart or closer together.", 'Resource breadth: how many different resource types are available; narrow environments offer fewer options, so competitors overlap more.']
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a framework that combines modern coexistence theory with competition-induced phenotypic plasticity and evolution for two competing species, showing that the breadth of available resources determines whether divergent or convergent plasticity promotes or hinders coexistence.
summary.plain: Two species that compete for the same resources can either share the living space or one can wipe out the other; ecologists have good tools for predicting this, but those tools mostly ignore that organisms can change their traits within their lifetimes in response to competitors, as well as evolving over generations. The authors write down a mathematical framework that includes both kinds of change for two competing species, and study how it plays out when the range of available resources is broad versus narrow. From the abstract, they report that in broad environments, plastic changes that push the species apart speed up the move toward coexistence, while in narrower environments the same kind of change can instead lead to one species being excluded.
summary.why: It matters because it suggests that short-term, reversible trait responses can change where long-term evolution ends up, so studies that ignore plasticity may misjudge which species persist. The abstract does not show empirical tests, so its practical reach is unclear; it may connect to work on how biodiversity responds to rapid environmental change.

title: Phenotypic plasticity reshapes the evolution of species coexistence

abstract: Pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) is classically associated with an extracellular respiratory burst generated by plasma membrane-localized NADPH oxidases (RBOHs). Here, we identify an ancient RBOH-independent intracellular respiratory burst driven by central carbon metabolism. Using in vivo biosensors, we demonstrate that receptor activation rapidly triggers sugar catabolism via glycolysis, shifting the NAD pool toward its reduced state. This redox pressure drives a burst in mitochondrial respiratory flux and oxygen consumption. Consequent mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production activates ANAC017-mediated retrograde signaling to induce broader PTI gene expression. This intracellular respiratory burst represents a conserved early hallmark of immunity across land plants and links cellular carbon status to immune activation. It reveals functional parallels between plant immune metabolism and metabolic reprogramming during mammalian immune-cell activation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767486 v1

title: The intracellular respiratory burst of plant immunity signaling

abstract: The plant nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors are known to play a crucial role in plant host defence against a variety of biotic stresses. Several NLR proteins contain integrated domains (NLR-ID) like ankyrin (ANK) and WRKY transcription factor domains and are important evolutionary adaptations in plant immunity. They are responsible for the perception of effector molecules from invading pathogens and pests and subsequent activation of plant immune responses. However, the functional roles these ANK-NLR-WRKY proteins play in wheat (Triticum aestivum) against various pathogens and pests remain poorly understood. Computational tools employed for comparative sequence and phylogenetic analyses revealed that TaAdnr1 is highly conserved across diploid (T. urartu), tetraploid (T. dicoccoides), and hexaploid (T. aestivum) wheat species, including its well characterised orthologue YrU1 from T. urartu. Three-dimensional (3D) protein structural modelling using AlphaFold2 supported strong conservation in the multiple domains of these NLR orthologues, more specifically within the integrated WRKY domain. This conservation may suggest a strong evolutionary maintenance of TaADNR1. Furthermore, this may also suggest TaADNR1 reflects specificity in effector recognition and regulation. Therefore, the integration of functional genomics studies, sequence analysis, evolutionary analysis and structural modelling possesses the potential to provide new insights into the pleiotropic roles of integrated domain NLRs in wheat.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767528 v1

abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) is an important medicinal cannabinoid which accumulates in the Cannabis sativa plant as the precursor cannabidiolic acid (CBDA). Measurement of CBDA levels is important for crop valuation, harvest optimisation, and quality control. However, its quantification typically requires laboratory-based analytical methods that are not readily deployable at the point of need. Here, we report the development of an engineered protein biosensor for selective CBDA detection based on chemically induced dimerization of engineered nanobody domains. Here a cannabidiol-responsive nanobody pair was incorporated into a two-component beta-lactamase-based biosensor architecture, such that ligand binding ultimately results in reconstitution of beta-lactamase activity quantified in a simple colorimetric assay. The resulting sensor displayed high affinity for CBD (KD = 1.9 +/- 0.2 nM) and CBDA (KD = 32 +/- 4 nM). Structure analysis informed a single substitution mutation of ligand-binding nanobody to shift its selectivity in favour of CBDA. This minimal modification inverted sensor specificity, generating a CBDA-selective biosensor that showed no detectable activation either by CBD or the immediate biosynthetic precursor, cannabigerolic acid (CBGA). The engineered sensor exhibited nanomolar affinity for CBDA (KD = 21 +/- 2.4 nM), an 8.4-fold dynamic range, and a limit of detection of 0.5 nM. Sensor performance was validated using crude extracts from CBDA-producing biomass and achieved 95.6% agreement with LCMS-based quantification.

abstract: Inherited retinal diseases are leading candidates for gene therapy, but photoreceptor-directed adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors still require subretinal injection, which treats only part of the retina and carries surgical risk. Intravitreal delivery is simple and panretinal, yet inner-retinal barriers block most capsids, and capsids selected in one species rarely translate. Mapping retinal glycans across seven mammals, we found heparan sulfate (HS) marking the inner limiting membrane and terminal N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) enriched on photoreceptor segments. These invariants defined a two-part design principle, attenuated HS binding with strong terminal GlcNAc engagement, implemented as a sequential in vitro selection, Conserved Receptor-Selection Technology (CReST). Its lead GlcNAc-selected capsid, AAV2.IvtB, increased retinal transgene expression 6.5-fold over AAV2.7m8 in mice and photoreceptor transduction 2.5-fold in pigs, acting through terminal GlcNAc engagement. It partially preserved photoreceptors in rd10 mice and suppressed laser-induced choroidal neovascularization. CReST is a receptor-guided, animal-free route to capsids with a defined, conserved mechanism.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767272 v1

abstract: Purpose Suicide during pregnancy or after birth (the perinatal period) represents a leading, preventable cause of United States maternal deaths. This study aimed to understand the complex relationship between perinatal status and life circumstances among perinatal suicide decedents in the United States and generate insights regarding suicide risk. Methods This cross-sectional study used decedent data from the 2003-2023 National Violent Death Reporting System suicide mortality registry (N=20,217). We applied psychometric network analysis using 18 binary life circumstances indicators representing four domains: relationships, health, socioeconomic status, and risk factors for suicide. We generated two networks for the overall sample and perinatal sample and assessed network structure, bridge centralities, and stability. Results The analytic sample included 1,297 perinatal and 18,920 non-perinatal decedents. The network of the overall sample was stable. Perinatal status did not appear at the center of the network but connected primarily with intimate partner problems. The network of the perinatal sample was modestly stable. Postpartum status was not at the center of the network but connected to depressed mood and mental health diagnoses. In both networks, depressed mood had the highest bridge betweenness, and there was a consistent link between physical health domains and socioeconomic domains. Conclusion Suicide prevention strategies targeting childbearing-aged women should incorporate factors beyond pregnancy, including physical health, intimate partner relationships, and socioeconomic challenges.

abstract: Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is an increasingly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition with multifactorial origins, including potential prenatal environmental contributions. Maternal anemia (decreased hemoglobin [Hb] levels) has long been associated with adverse offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes. Yet, evidence regarding elevated levels of antenatal hemoglobin levels, in relation to ASD risk remains limited. This study evaluated the association between maternal Hb levels during pregnancy and the risk of ASD diagnosis in offspring. Methods This large-scale, population-based retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from births of members of Clalit Health Services (CHS), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, between 2011 and 2021. The study included 303,234 singleton live births to Jewish mothers who had at least one measured prenatal Hb value and were CHS members. Exclusion criteria were children with known genetic disorders and births <25 weeks of gestation. Maternal Hb, and red blood cells (RBC) levels during the first and second trimesters were categorized as low (<2.5th percentile), normal (reference), or high (>97.5th percentile). The main outcome was a diagnosis of ASD in the offspring, as recorded in medical files. Statistical analyses adjusted for maternal age, socioeconomic status, gestational diabetes, BMI, and other clinical and demographic factors. Results Among the 303,234 births, 8,106 (2.7%) children were diagnosed with ASD. High maternal Hb levels were associated with elevated odds of ASD diagnosis (aOR=1.22; 95% CI=1.08:1.37), with the strongest association observed for first-trimester measurements (aOR=1.31; 95% CI=1.14-1.49). This association persisted in the sibling-matched analysis (aOR=1.64; 95% CI=1.08-2.47) and was not modified by maternal RBC levels, suggesting that it was not explained by familial factors or RBC counts. The main limitations of this study include the lack of available data on maternal smoking, and the absence of detailed information on maternal nutritional status. Conclusions These findings suggest that elevated antenatal Hb levels may be relevant to offspring neurodevelopment. Further studies are needed to replicate these findings and clarify the biological mechanisms underlying this association.

abstract: BackgroundHistorically, the Variola virus caused deadly smallpox epidemics in children. In Copenhagen, transmission was halted by 1810 when [~]90% of children were vaccinated following the introduction of a mandatory single-dose vaccine program. A 14-year honeymoon period followed, but in 1824 smallpox re-emerged as a milder disease of adults. We set out to study smallpox epidemics between 1824 and 1835 when all smallpox patients in Copenhagen were quarantined. MethodWe analyze data from 3795 smallpox patients reported by the treating physicians between 1824 and 1835. The data include age, vaccination status, and outcome. We estimate age-specific case fatality ratios (CFR) and vaccine effectiveness (VE) against mortality. FindingsFor the four outbreaks while quarantine was mandatory (1824-1834), the CFR was [~]1% among the vaccinated and [~]25% among the unvaccinated, corresponding to a VE of [~]95%. For the fifth outbreak in 1835, we found that CFR was low among the vaccinated but increased with age, which is evidence of waning vaccine protection. Almost no cases were over 40 years of age, suggesting lifelong immunity from smallpox infection. InterpretationAs the unvaccinated CFR was high and comparable to the pre-vaccine era, the milder post-honeymoon smallpox disease cannot be explained by genetic changes in the virus. Rather, high coverage with an effective vaccine combined with waning vaccine protection in adulthood explains the changing face of smallpox. We demonstrates how high vaccine coverage can disguise an outbreak of highly pathogenic smallpox as the milder Variola minor.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368180 v1

title: The effect of smallpox vaccination: unique insights gained from Danish post-honeymoon epidemics 200 years ago

abstract: The upper respiratory tract (URT) microbiome modulates the local mucosal immune environment, with potential implications for respiratory viral infection susceptibility and outcomes. We leveraged a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study in 34 healthy young adults, 18 of whom became infected, to characterize host gene expression and microbiome composition and dynamics in nasal and throat samples collected before viral inoculation and over the subsequent 14 days. Compared with participants who remained uninfected, participants who became infected had elevated baseline nasal expression of gene modules related to interferon, innate inflammatory, and neutrophil responses, as well as a delayed transcriptional response to viral challenge. Baseline nasal microbiome composition differed modestly by subsequent infection status, with lower relative abundances of Corynebacterium accolens and higher abundances of Dolosigranulum pigrum and Staphylococcus aureus among participants who became infected. Integrated analyses of microbiome and host gene expression data identified coordinated networks of microbiome features and host immune modules that distinguished infected from uninfected participants, including prior to inoculation. Notably, immune modules associated with infection susceptibility were positively correlated with S. aureus abundance and negatively correlated with the abundances of common nasal commensals, Corynebacterium spp. and Staphylococcus epidermidis, linking altered nasal microbiome community structure with the heightened inflammatory state associated with infection susceptibility. Symptom burden and viral load were similarly linked to distinct networks of microbiome and host gene expression features within nasal samples. Taken together, these findings highlight potential microbiome-host interactions within the nasal mucosa that may contribute to differences in respiratory viral infection outcomes.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368138 v1

summary.plain: Some people catch a respiratory virus after exposure while others do not, and the reasons are not well understood. Researchers deliberately exposed healthy volunteers to SARS-CoV-2 and sampled their noses and throats for two weeks, both before and after exposure. They found that people who later became infected already differed in their nasal immune activity and in the mix of bacteria living in their noses before any virus was given.
summary.why: Because the study records people before they are exposed, it can look for early markers of susceptibility rather than only describing infection after the fact. The links it reports are correlations among many measured features, so they point to possible microbe-immune interactions worth testing rather than establishing a cause; the abstract alone does not show how strong or reproducible these links are.

title: Upper respiratory microbiome and host immune signatures associated with SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and illness in a human challenge model

abstract: Brazil is one of the higher meat producer and consumer worldwide. Recently, the sustainability of the meat market is questioned on regard to its high contribution to climate change and public health concerns such as obesity. Hence, further public policies are likely to regulate the meat market and simultaneously reduce meat production and consumption. However, in the context of middle-income countries marked by strong inequalities such as Brazil, the nutritional effect of such market regulation is uncertain. Indeed, one can hypothesize that meat intake plays a protective role against poor nutritious food intake and weight gain among underprivileged settings. To test this hypothesis, this study analyzes household cross-sectional yearly surveys collected from 2018 to 2023 in the 27 Brazilian State capitals. As expected, multivariate estimates show education-specific associations between meat intake and obesity. Among the most educated individuals, declaring not consuming any meat the previous day before the survey is associated with lower body mass index (BMI) and obesity risk, as observed in previous epidemiological studies. By contrast, declaring consuming meat the previous day before the survey appears to be protective against weight gain among poorly educated individuals. We also observe education-specific meat substitution behaviors that help explain these findings. In facts, meat is more likely to be replaced by sweets and ready-to-eat meals among poorly educated individuals compared to more educated ones. We conclude that, everything being equals, meat market regulation policy might worsen public health concerns for under-privileged individuals. Important investments in the education sector and anti-poverty programs are thus needed to limit the raise of nutritional inequalities.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368245 v1

title: Does educational attainment change the association between meat intake and obesity? A case-study from urban Brazil.

abstract: Background: Tuberculosis Diagnosis delays among tuberculosis patients can worsen infection transmission, disease severity, and mortality risk. Identifying factors influencing delays is crucial due to its persistence across healthcare levels and communities. The study identify determinants of tuberculosis diagnosis delay among patients attending public health facility of Metekel zone, Northwest Ethiopia:2023 Methods: An unmatched case-control study was conducted in Metekel zone health facilities from March to April 2023, involving 210 tuberculosis patients (103 cases, 107 controls) selected through systematic sampling. Data collected through structured questionnaires and STATA used for analysis, including bi-variable and multi-variable logistic regressions. Variables with p-value < 0.25 in bi-variable analysis were included in the final model after checking model fitness and multicollinearity. Results: Overall, 210 tuberculosis patients were included in the study. The following independent variables were associated diagnosis delay of tuberculosis: TB patients who travel greater than 10km (AOR: 2.941, (95 % CI: 1.509, 5.731); TB patients who are living at rural area (AOR: 4.135, 95 % CI :1.759, 9.723); TB patients who prior visit in holly-water and traditional medicine [AOR: 2.978, (95% CI: 1.292, 6.863); poor knowledge about TB [AOR: 2.826, (95% CI: 1.404, 5.687)]. Conclusion: Tuberculosis diagnosis delay is a major challenge to eliminate tuberculosis by breaking the chain of transmission. This study can be attributed to factors including place of residence being rural, poor knowledge about tuberculosis, non-health facility initial actions upon symptom onset, and far distance to health institutions. Recognizing these determinants helps in identifying and addressing barriers inhibiting early diagnosis, potentially improving healthcare access and promoting more timely diagnosis and treatment for tuberculosis patients.

abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) effectively treats motor and non-motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). However, 15-20 % of patients experience postoperative cognitive decline and identifying preoperative markers remains an unmet clinical need. In this prospective open-label study, we employed NODDI-DTI to investigate whether cerebral microstructure predicts cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS. Forty PD patients underwent diffusion MRI and neuropsychological assessments at preoperative baseline and 6-month follow-up. A whole-brain voxel-wise analysis related microstructural metrics to postoperative cognitive change. Compromised microstructure within three large-scale networks - the frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual networks - was associated with greater postoperative cognitive decline. These findings suggest that both disease-related network degeneration and stimulation acting on compromised circuits may contribute to postoperative cognitive decline. In conclusion, preoperative evaluation of microstructural integrity may help identify patients at risk for postoperative cognitive decline, supporting individualised counselling and targeted behavioural monitoring after STN-DBS.

abstract: Objectives: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers offer an opportunity to characterize Parkinson's disease (PD) biology. The objective of this study was to investigate such biomarkers in deeply-phenotyped participants in Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). Methods: Baseline plasma samples from early (<2 years since diagnosis) sporadic PD participants with a positive CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA) and healthy controls (HC) with a negative aSyn-SAA test were utilized. Plasma P-tau217 (Roche Diagnostics), neurofilament light chain (NfL, Quanterix), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, Quanterix), and (PD only) amyloid-beta (A{beta}) levels (40 and 42, C2N Diagnostics) were measured. Clinical features at baseline and over up to 11 years were compared across biomarker tertiles in models controlling for age, sex, and baseline outcome variable. Results: The cohort was 97 HC and 523 PD and participants. Median [IQR] biomarker values (pg/mL) for HC and PD were P-tau217: 0.14 [0.06 -0.75], 0.15 [0.06 -0.90]; NfL: 10.6 [3.13 -49.85], 12.26 [3.77-62.67]; GFAP: 66.56 [19.75 -403.48], 87.19 [14.55 -531.82]; and in PD A{beta}40: 391.32 [209.95 -538.38]; A{beta}42: 42.74[27.75 -68.55]. No biomarkers differed between HC and PD. In PD, biomarkers were associated with age. In PD only, higher baseline levels of P-tau217 and NfL were associated with greater hazards of a worse cognitive and balance outcome. P-tau217, NfL, and GFAP levels were associated with change in cognitive score over time. Interpretation: Plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels in early, sporadic PD with confirmed synucleinopathy predict future cognitive and functional impairment, and these findings can inform clinical research design and clinical care.

abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) genomic studies have largely underrepresented African populations, limiting understanding of disease biology in these groups. This study addressed this gap by generating integrated genomic and transcriptomic data from South African (SA) CRC patients, establishing a foundation for future cancer studies. Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 samples identified several differentially expressed genes between tumour and normal samples, with AGAP3, AMPD2, ANKRD10, and SALL4 showing strong diagnostic performance (average sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 94.22%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 89.5%). SALL4 performed best and was validated using TCGA data and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Consensus Molecular Subtype classification revealed a distinct distribution, with enrichment of metabolic (CMS3, 30%) and mesenchymal (CMS4, 30%) subtypes and under-representation of canonical CMS2 (21%). APC mutation rates were lower than in European patients (~55% vs ~75%). Functional analysis identified inflammatory pathways as primary drivers of carcinogenesis, with viral influences exacerbating the inflammatory tumour microenvironment. Altered neural pathways in tumour samples suggested a consequential gut-brain axis loop as cancer infiltrates enervated tissue, an increasingly relevant field to which these data contribute. Whole-genome sequencing of 12 samples revealed pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with transcriptomic differential expression; SMPD1, PERM1, PRRT2, and RP1 emerged as potential multi-omics markers, while novel mutations (KDM6A, C2CD2, TAF2, SLC6A16, OR5M10, PITRM1, TRIM64B, CARD11) were identified as previously unrecognised contributors to CRC progression in African samples. These findings expand genomic resources for African cancer research and provide new insights into the molecular landscape and tumourigenesis mechanisms of CRC in SA patients, supporting the development of population-specific precision oncology approaches.

abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality, with a minority of patients experiencing durable responses to first-line immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Currently, there are no easily accessible tools to predict clinical benefit to first-line immunotherapy. To address this gap, we developed LCatlas (https://www.lcatlas.org), a point-of-care web application designed to predict immunotherapy outcomes and inform evidence-based treatment decisions. Using data from 79 NSCLC patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, we extracted demographic, clinical, and molecular features from electronic medical records and compared three independent approaches, statistical model (logistic regression), machine learning (XGboost), and AI model (TabTransformer) to identify the most effective predictor. LCatlas accepts nine variables, gender, smoking history, bone/pleura/liver metastasis, PDL1 tumor staining, albumin level, hemoglobin level, lymphocyte count, neutrophil count, and platelet count, to predict responses to both immunotherapy and immunotherapy plus chemotherapy. LCatlas cross-validation yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 79% [72% - 85%], with sensitivity of 87% [72% - 95%] and specificity of 78% [64% - 89%], outperforming previous studies including high-volume data-driven deep-learning approaches. In a validation cohort consisting of 28 individuals, it demonstrated a prediction accuracy of 82%. LCatlas may serve as a valuable point-of-care tool by identifying patients likely to experience extended immunotherapy or combination therapy using readily available medical data. Its evidence-based approach can optimize personalized treatment planning and thereby promote quality and safety of care.

abstract: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

abstract: Objectives: To examine how quickly software vulnerabilities are exploited after public disclosure, and whether hacking breaches at US health care providers changed in size after 2021, a period in which earlier studies had found attacks concentrating on large organizations. Methods: Retrospective analysis of public data. We linked the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (1,748 entries) with CVE publication dates to measure time to confirmed exploitation by half-year of publication (2021-2025). We also analyzed 8,029 breach reports submitted to the HHS Office for Civil Rights, focusing on hacking/IT incidents at health care providers. Results: Median time to confirmed exploitation was 24 days for vulnerabilities published from late 2021 to mid 2022, 0 days for those published in the second half of 2022, and 6 days in 2023-2025, with no further shortening across 2023-2025 (P = .40). About a quarter were exploited on or before the day of disclosure. Among provider hacking breaches, the share affecting fewer than 5,000 people fell from 42% in 2016 to 32% in 2022 (trend P = .004) and rose to 46% in 2025 (P < .001). Conclusions: The window between disclosure and exploitation had narrowed to about a week before generative AI was widely available. After 2022, breaches moved toward smaller events, reversing the earlier concentration on large organizations. Defenses that depend on patching speed will not protect small providers.

abstract: An institution must complete a portfolio adjustment, but traders who prepare inventory for it can choose whether to participate. We study how public forecasts affect the institution's cost in a Bayesian execution game with optional activation, transient impact, and uniform-price terminal completion. The curvature of equilibrium cost as a function of the posterior target mean determines the value of information. In the scalar model, information benefits every fixed participation roster. Optional supply can reverse this ranking at entry, at full participation, and in a smooth interior with lognormal activation costs. For centered scalar targets, information weakly lowers cost relative to no information, strictly when the posterior mean is nonzero with positive probability. Centered Gaussian precision gains are always beneficial. An exact symmetric finite-population equilibrium identifies how information resolution and individual strategic size interact near entry. A portfolio extension gives a matrix criterion for the fixed-roster ranking, which can fail under general cross-impact. Even with isotropic execution, shared activation allows equally accurate signals about target magnitude and composition to have opposite execution values under one unchanged prior. Intraday ETF price data is used to characterize target uncertainty and trading conditions without identifying activation or institutional costs.

abstract: This article extends the forward rate curve model of Baaquie and Bouchaud (2004) and Le Coz and Bouchaud (2024) to the multi-country setting of government bond markets. Cross-country blocks of correlation matrices of realized yield changes are found to display significant asymmetry between maturities. In the framework of the proposed model, this amounts to give to each country an idiosyncratic time scale. Each time scale describes how the perceived time between future dates depends on the dates themselves. The differences between these time scales structure the interactions between curves and reproduce the characteristic asymmetry of cross-country correlation matrices. The proposed model captures the full set of cross-curve correlations simultaneously at both daily and intra-day frequencies. When calibrated on government bonds issued by nine countries of the euro-zone, the typical reconstruction error is 1.7%.

abstract: Decision fusion combines local decisions from distributed sensors to support reliable detection of phenomena in wireless networks. The effectiveness of decision fusion depends on sensing accuracy, reporting-channel reliability, and available communications and computation resources. This article surveys decision-fusion techniques for wireless sensor networks and emerging communication systems, bringing together their theoretical foundations and practical implementation requirements. We review network architectures and hard, soft, and quantized reporting strategies, and examine statistical, learning-based, game-theoretic, and heuristic fusion approaches. Advanced fusion techniques, including relay-aware combining, link-adaptive regeneration, branch selection, and likelihood approximations, are discussed with emphasis on their assumptions, information requirements, and limitations. The survey examines tradeoffs among detection performance, computational complexity, communications overhead, energy consumption, and latency. The tradeoffs are considered across representative sensing applications and emerging technologies, including massive machine-type communication, ultra-reliable low-latency communication, uncrewed aerial vehicle-assisted networks, and the massive Internet of Things. The reviewed literature highlights the importance of jointly considering sensing quality, reporting reliability, and fusion processing when selecting a suitable strategy. Finally, we identify research directions in resource-aware optimization, uncertainty calibration, and robust learning-based fusion under heterogeneous data, missing reports, and changing wireless conditions. Particular attention is given to convergence, generalization, and the costs of training and inference.

abstract: This paper investigates the adaptive codebook design for task-oriented token communication over wireless networks with dynamic channels. This paper proposes the channel-aware codebook (CAC), a joint channel- and reconstruction-driven framework that reorders the labels of a frozen 14-bit VQGAN codebook. In the considered framework, a balanced geometric partition forms prefix groups, a prefix bijection places the groups on the label hypercube, and bijective suffix assignments place the codewords within each group. The problem is formulated to minimize the expected full-image perceptual distortion of the frozen decoder under a binary symmetric channel, averaged over a design set of bit error rates (BERs) and retaining simultaneous token errors. An offline algorithm alternates prefix and suffix exchanges and screens and confirms candidates on paired batches under a fixed decoder-evaluation budget. The assignment preserves the error-free reconstruction and the payload and deploys as static lookup tables without retraining. Under the binary symmetric channel at BER $0.01$, it reduces LPIPS by $12.3\%$ and improves COCO AP by $14.1\%$ ($1.72$ points) relative to the native labels, and it lowers LPIPS by a further $4.5\%$ relative to a related assignment adaptation at the same payload.
label: arXiv:2611.26038v1

abstract: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible target speech together with diverse environmental sounds as a coherent acoustic scene. The task is considered challenging in two respects. Speech and environmental audio differ substantially in their semantic and acoustic characteristics, yet existing approaches typically model the complete scene using a single mixed acoustic representation. At the same time, the two sounds are closely related in real-world speech scenes, whereas conventional approaches usually rely on simulated scenes mixed from independently recorded sources. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based framework for joint modeling of distinct speech and environment token streams. A source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both token streams in an interleaved fashion conditioned on the natural-language scene description and speech content. This formulation preserves source-specific representations while modeling the token streams within a shared generative context. Since both streams are extracted directly from mixed recordings, the model can also be adapted to in-the-wild speech scenes without isolated sources. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation techniques, with consistent gains from real-world adaptation. We further investigate the effects of distinct token representations and interleaved generation, and analyze whether the environmental sound remains stable while speech is active and how the two streams interact.
label: arXiv:2611.25503v1

summary.background: ['Neural audio codec: a model that compresses audio into a short sequence of discrete tokens and can reconstruct sound from them.', 'Language model generation over tokens: large language models can be trained to predict audio tokens, as they predict words in text.', 'Interleaved generation: producing two token streams alternately, so each can take the other into account as it is built.', 'Speech-scene generation: creating a full soundscape with clear speech plus background sounds that match a scene description.', 'Simulated versus in-the-wild data: simulated scenes mix separately recorded sources, while in-the-wild recordings are natural and cannot be cleanly separated, which is why extracting sources from mixtures matters.', 'Intelligibility and scene relevance: standard goals in evaluating generated speech (can it be understood) and generated scenes (do they match the description).']
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes an LLM-based system that jointly generates separate speech and environmental-sound token streams, extracted from mixed recordings by a source-aware neural audio codec, so that speech and background audio form one coherent acoustic scene, including for real-world recordings without isolated sources.
summary.plain: The task is to produce a realistic audio scene in which someone speaks clearly and the surrounding sounds, such as traffic or a room's ambience, fit with that setting. The authors treat speech and background sound as two separate sequences of compressed audio codes and have a language model generate both, interleaved, from a text description of the scene and the words to be spoken. Because the training data comes directly from mixed real recordings rather than artificially layered clips, the approach can be adapted to messy, in-the-wild audio; the abstract reports gains in intelligibility, scene relevance and audio quality over existing methods, but gives no specific figures here.
summary.why: Generating speech and its environment together, rather than as a simulated mix, could matter for audio content creation, dubbing, and training data for speech systems that must cope with noisy settings. The abstract does not show how large the improvements are or how well they hold beyond the authors' tests, so the practical significance is not yet clear.

title: Joint Language Modeling for In-the-Wild Speech-Scene Generation with Distinct Token Representations

abstract: Ultra-low-bitrate speech coding is crucial for bandwidth-constrained communication and compact storage, but preserving intelligibility, naturalness, and fine-grained acoustic details at bitrates of only a few hundred bps remains challenging. Existing purely acoustic codecs generally operate at relatively high bitrates, whereas incorporating semantic representations can reduce the bitrate, but at the cost of increased complexity. Therefore, we propose UMelCodec, a purely acoustic neural speech codec operating in the mel domain at an ultra-low bitrate of 325 bps with a lightweight architecture. UMelCodec consists of two stages. In the first mel-domain coding stage, alias-free Snake-ConvNeXt (AF-SC) encoder-decoder backbones model temporal and harmonic structures, a factorized single-codebook vector quantizer (VQ) enables ultra-low-bitrate quantization, and a multi-scale mel-spectrogram discriminator (MSMD) improves mel-spectrogram reconstruction. In the second waveform synthesis stage, a lightweight modified discrete cosine transform (MDCT)-based neural vocoder predicts the MDCT spectrum from the reconstructed mel spectrogram and recovers the waveform through inverse MDCT. Experiments on LibriTTS dataset demonstrate that UMelCodec outperforms strong baselines across most objective reconstruction metrics while maintaining competitive subjective naturalness. In terms of model complexity and inference efficiency, UMelCodec has only 19.67 M parameters, requires 1.93 G MACs, and supports real-time inference on both GPU and CPU platforms.
label: arXiv:2611.25569v1

summary.one_liner: Ultra-low-bitrate speech coding is crucial for bandwidth-constrained communication and compact storage, but preserving intelligibility, naturalness, and fine-grained acoustic details at bitrates of only a few hundred bps remains challenging.

title: UMelCodec: An Ultra-Low-Bitrate and Lightweight Mel-Domain Neural Speech Codec

abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) applies only the first input of an optimized sequence before replanning. Do the available data determine this input? We define first-action informativity as agreement across data-compatible models at a fixed history and reference, with common MPC settings. For autoregressive models with exogenous inputs (ARX) and unconstrained quadratic MPC, we show that first-action agreement and prediction agreement under a fixed input sequence do not imply one another. We give structural conditions for action agreement without requiring unique model identification. When actions disagree, we quantify their mean-squared deviation from the fitted model's input under a specific parameter distribution. We approximate this measure using local sensitivities and parameter covariance. Analytical and numerical examples illustrate how model uncertainty affects predictions and actions differently. The framework evaluates model uncertainty through its effect on the first action MPC is about to apply.
label: arXiv:2611.25319v1

summary.background: ['Model predictive control (MPC): at each time step, optimize a sequence of future inputs over a horizon, apply only the first, then re-optimize.', 'ARX model: a linear model that predicts the current output from past outputs and past inputs, plus exogenous (external) inputs.', 'System identification: estimating model parameters from recorded input-output data; a model is identified when the data determine its parameters uniquely.', 'Parameter covariance: a measure of how uncertain the estimated parameters are, typically from the fitting procedure.', 'Local sensitivity: how much an output (here, the first control action) changes when a parameter changes slightly, approximated by derivatives.', "Mean-squared deviation: the average of squared differences, used here to measure how far alternative models' actions stray from the fitted model's action."]
summary.one_liner: The paper asks whether data-compatible ARX models agree on the first input an unconstrained quadratic MPC would apply, shows that first-action agreement and multi-step prediction agreement are logically distinct, gives structural conditions for action agreement without unique identification, and approximates the action disagreement via local sensitivities and parameter covariance.
summary.plain: Model predictive control repeatedly plans a sequence of control inputs but only uses the first one before planning again. The authors ask whether the recorded data are enough to pin down that single first input, even when the data do not pin down the whole underlying model. They report that agreement on the first action and agreement on long-range predictions can come apart, and they offer a way to measure how much the uncertain model shifts that first action.
summary.why: It targets a gap between how well a learned model predicts the future and whether it leads to the same decision, which matters for anyone deploying data-driven controllers. The abstract does not show practical impact beyond the analytical and numerical examples it mentions, so its reach beyond ARX models with unconstrained quadratic MPC is unclear.

title: The Prediction-to-Decision Gap: First-Action Informativity in Data-Driven Predictive Control

abstract: Constrained regulation of the internal state of an unknown linear system is challenging when only input-output measurements are available online. In this work, we develop a data-enabled output-feedback predictive control (DeoPC) framework for constrained state regulation using input-output data. Specifically, a data-driven state estimate is constructed from past input-output data via a subspace-based singular value decomposition. Based on this state representation, we formulate a predictive controller that directly penalizes the state and control effort while enforcing the system constraints. Under persistent excitation and initialization conditions, we establish recursive feasibility and closed-loop stability of DeoPC in both noise-free and bounded-noise settings. In addition, we show that DeoPC can be calibrated to the physical state coordinates using a few offline state measurements, or treated as a model predictive control tuning problem when no state measurements are available. The effectiveness of DeoPC is demonstrated through simulations on an unstable batch reactor system.
label: arXiv:2611.25465v1

summary.background: ['State: the set of internal variables that together determine how a system will evolve; often not directly measured.', 'Linear system: one whose input-output behaviour can be described by linear equations.', 'Output feedback: control that uses only measured outputs, not the full internal state.', 'Model predictive control (MPC): at each step, optimise a plan over a short future horizon subject to constraints, apply the first action, then repeat.', 'Recursive feasibility: the guarantee that the optimisation problem stays solvable at every future step, so the controller never gets stuck.', "Persistent excitation: the requirement that the recorded input data is varied enough to reveal the system's behaviour.", 'Singular value decomposition (SVD): a matrix factorisation used here to extract the dominant patterns in recorded data.', 'Batch reactor: a chemical vessel processed in discrete batches; used as a test case for an unstable process.']
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes DeoPC, a data-driven output-feedback model predictive controller that estimates an unknown linear system's internal state from past input-output data via SVD-based subspace methods and enforces constraints, with recursive feasibility and closed-loop stability shown under persistent excitation and initialization conditions.
summary.plain: Engineers often need to keep a machine's hidden internal condition within safe limits, but they can only see what goes in and what comes out, and they may not have a mathematical model of the machine. This paper builds a controller that reconstructs the hidden internal state from recent input and output records and then chooses future control actions that respect limits. The abstract reports theoretical guarantees that the controller keeps working and stays stable under stated data conditions, with and without bounded measurement noise, and tests it in simulation on an unstable batch reactor.
summary.why: It addresses a practical gap: controlling a system whose internal state is hidden and whose model is unknown, using only data. The approach may matter to process industries and anyone who wants model-free control with safety constraints, though the abstract does not show how it compares with existing data-driven methods on real hardware.

title: DeoPC: Data-Enabled Output-Feedback Predictive Control for State Regulation
